parts.problemMd:
(i) Factorise $2t^{2}+5t+2$.

[2]

(ii) $t$ is a positive whole number.

The expression $2t^{2}+5t+2$ can never have a value that is a prime number.
Explain why.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *Multiply 2 by 2 (the first number by the last number)*

*2 × 2 = 4*

*Find two numbers that multiply to give 4 and add to give 5 (the middle number)*

*4 and 1*

*Split the middle term into 4**t** and **t*

$2t^{2}+4t+t+2$

*Factorise fully the first pair of terms and the second pair of terms *

$2 t \left(t + 2\right) + 1 \left(t + 2\right)$

**[1]**

> *Factorise out the whole (**t** + 2) bracket as if it were one term, leaving 2**t** and +1 in their own bracket *

$\left(t + 2\right) \left(2 t + 1\right)$

$(t+2)(2t+1)$ **[1]**

ii) *Write the expression in factorised form* * *

$2 t^{2} + 5 t + 2 = \left(t + 2\right) \left(2 t + 1\right)$ * *

*Find out what values (**t** + 2) can take* * *

*If ***t*** is a positive whole number then (***t*** + 2) will be a positive whole number greater than 2* * *

*Find out what values (2**t** + 1) can take* * *

*If ***t*** is a positive whole number then (2***t*** + 1) is a positive (odd) number greater than 1*

*Prime numbers only have factors of 1 and themselves (and cannot be written as the product of any other two numbers) Explain why (**t** + 2)(2**t** + 1) cannot be prime * * *

**(****t**** + 2)(2****t**** + 1) will always be the product of two numbers greater than 1 so can never be a prime number ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Prove that

$\left(2 n  +  3\right)^{2}  -  \left(2 n  -  3\right)^{2}$  is a multiple of $8$

for all positive integer values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Expand (2**n** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* * * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(2 n + 3\right) \left(2 n + 3\right) \\ & = & 4 n^{2} + 6 n + 6 n + 9 \\ & = & 4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9\end{aligned}$ * *

*Expand (2**n** - 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* * * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n - 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(2 n - 3\right) \left(2 n - 3\right) \\ & = & 4 n^{2} - 6 n - 6 n + 9 \\ & = & 4 n^{2} - 12 n + 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Put these results in brackets and subtract the second from the first* * *

$\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n - 3\right)^{2} = \left(4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9\right) - \left(4 n^{2} - 12 n + 9\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side* *Collect "like" terms* * *

$4n^{2}+12n+9-4n^{2}+12n-9\,=24n$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is a multiple of 8 (by writing it as 8 × "an integer" )* * *

$8\times3n$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then 3**n** will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 8 × "an integer"* * *

$8\times3n$** is a multiple of 8 for all positive integer values of ****n**** ****[1]**

*Method 2*

*The "difference of two squares" says **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2 *</sup>*= (**a **+ **b**)(**a** - **b**) Factorise (2**n** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - (2**n** - 3)*<sup>*2 *</sup>*using the "difference of two squares" where** a** = 2**n** + 3 and **b** = 2**n** - 3* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n - 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(\left(2 n + 3\right) + \left(2 n - 3\right)\right) \times \left(\left(2 n + 3\right) - \left(2 n - 3\right)\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the brackets on the right-hand side* * *

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(2 n + 3 + 2 n - 3\right) \left(2 n + 3 - 2 n + 3\right) \\ & = & \left(4 n\right) \left(6\right) \\ & = & 24 n\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is a multiple of 8 (by writing it as 8 × "an integer" )* * *

$8\times3n$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then 3**n** will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 8 × "an integer"* * *

$8\times3n$** is a multiple of 8 for all positive integer values of ****n**** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Prove algebraically that

$(2n+1)^{2}-(2n+1)$ is an even number

for all positive integer values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Expand (2**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets)* * *

$( 2 n + 1 ) ^{2} = ( 2 n + 1 ) ( 2 n + 1 )$
equals 4 n squared plus 2 n plus 2 n plus 1 * *

*Collect "like" **n** terms* * *

$\left(2 n + 1\right)^{2} = 4 n^{2} + 4 n + 1$

**[1]**

*Substitute this result into the original expression* * *

$4 n^{2} + 4 n + 1 - \left(2 n + 1\right)$ * *

*Remove the brackets (by multiplying each term inside by -1)* * *

$4n^{2}+4n+1-2n-1$ * *

*Collect "like" terms* * *

$4n^{2}+2n$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is an even number (by writing it as 2 × ... )* * *

$2 \times \left(2 n^{2} + n\right)$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then this expression is always even (as it is 2 x "an integer")* * *

$2\times(2n^{2}+n)$** is an even number for all positive integer values of ****n*** ***[1]**

*Method 2*

*Factorise the whole bracket (2**n** + 1) out of the expression* * *

$\left(2 n + 1\right) \left[\left(2 n + 1\right) - 1\right]$

**[1]**

*Collect the terms inside the square brackets* * *

$( 2 n + 1 ) [ 2 n ]$
$=2 n\left(2 n + 1\right)$

**[1]**

> *Show that this is an even number (by writing it as 2 x "an integer")  *

> $2 \times n \left(2 n + 1\right)$*  *

*If **n** is a positive integer then **n**(2**n** + 1) will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 2 × "an integer"* * *

$2\timesn(2n+1)$* *** is an even number for all positive integer values of ****n ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$n$ is an integer.

Prove algebraically that the sum of  $\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)$ and $\frac{1}{2}(n+1)(n+2)$ is always a square number.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the sum of the two expressions*

$\frac{1}{2} n \left(n + 1\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)$ * *

> *Method 1** *

> *Expand the brackets*

$1 half ( n ^{2} + n ) + 1 half ( n ^{2} + n + 2 n + 2 )$
$= 1 half n ^{2} + 1 half n + 1 half ( n ^{2} + 3 n + 2 )$
equals 1 half n squared plus 1 half n plus 1 half n squared plus 3 over 2 n plus 1

**[1]**

> *Collect "like" terms*

$n^{2}+2n+1$

*This is meant to be a square number* *Factorise the quadratic expression*

$\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right)$

> *Write this as the "square" of a bracket*

$\left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

> *If **n** is an integer then (**n** + 1) is an integer so (**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* is a square number*

$(n+1)^{2}$** ****is a square number**** [1]**

> *Method 2 *

> *Factorise out the whole of *$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right)$* from both terms*

$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left[n + \left(n + 2\right)\right]$

**[1]**

> *Collect "like" terms*

$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)$

> *Factorise the 2 out of the second bracket (and multiply it by the half)*

> * *$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right)\times 2\left(n + 1\right)$
$=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\times\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right)$
$=\left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

> * If **n** is an integer then (**n** + 1) is an integer so (**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* is a square number*

$(n+1)^{2}$** ****is a square number**** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(n + 3\right)^{2}  -  \left(n - 3\right)^{2}$  is an even number for all positive integer values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Expand (**n** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets) and collect "like" terms* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 3\right) \\ & = & n^{2} + 3 n + 3 n + 9 \\ & = & n^{2} + 6 n + 9\end{aligned}$ * *

*Expand (**n** - 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets) and collect "like" terms* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n - 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(n - 3\right) \left(n - 3\right) \\ & = & n^{2} - 3 n - 3 n + 9 \\ & = & n^{2} - 6 n + 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Put these results in brackets and subtract the second from the first* * *

$\left(n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(n - 3\right)^{2} = \left(n^{2} + 6 n + 9\right) - \left(n^{2} - 6 n + 9\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side (multiplying each term in the last bracket by -1)* *Collect "like" terms* * *

$n^{2}+6n+9-n^{2}+6n-9\,=12n$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is an even number (by writing it as 2 × "an integer" )* * *

$2\times6n$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then 6**n** will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 2 × "an integer"* * *

$2\times6n$** is an even number for all positive integer values of ****n**** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Here are the first five terms of an arithmetic sequence.

7      13      19      25      31

Prove that the difference between the squares of any two terms of the sequence is always a multiple of 24.
parts.solutionMd:
*The **n**th term of a linear (arithmetic) sequence is **dn** + **b*

> *Find the common difference, **d** (the amount by which the sequence goes up each time)*

**d*** = 6*

> *Find **b** (either by finding the term before the first term shown, or by solving 6**n** + **b** = 7 when **n** = 1)*

**b*** = 7 - 6 = 1* * *

> *Write down the formula for the **n**th term of the sequence *

**n***th term = 6***n*** + 1*

**d or b correct**** [1]** 
**[1]**

*For any two terms in the sequence, we can write the "**n**th term" as one of them and the "**p**th term" as the other*

> *Write down the formula for the **p**th term of the sequence*

**p***th term = 6***p*** + 1* * *

> *Find an expression for the difference between the squares of the **n**th and the **p**th term*

$\left(6 n + 1\right)^{2} - \left(6 p + 1\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Expand (6**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>

> $\begin{aligned}\left(6 n + 1\right) \left(6 n + 1\right) & = & 36 n^{2} + 6 n + 6 n + 1 \\ & = & 36 n^{2} + 12 n + 1\end{aligned}$* *

> *Use this result to expand (6**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>*- (6**p** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>

> $\left(6 n + 1\right)^{2} - \left(6 p + 1\right)^{2} = \left(36 n^{2} + 12 n + 1\right) - \left(36 p^{2} + 12 p + 1\right)$* *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side*

> *Collect "like" terms*

$36n^{2}+12n+1-36p^{2}-12p-1\,=36n^{2}-36p^{2}+12n-12p$

**[1]**

> *This does not yet look like a multiple of 24 (further algebra is needed) *

> *Factorise the first two terms and the last two terms*

> $36 \left(n^{2} - p^{2}\right) + 12 \left(n - p\right)$* *

> *Use the difference of two squares to factorise **n*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **p*<sup>*2*</sup>* further*

$36 \left(n + p\right) \left(n - p\right) + 12 \left(n - p\right)$

> *Factorise out the 12 and (**n** - **p**) *

$12 \left(n - p\right) \left[3 \left(n + p\right) + 1\right]$

> *As **n** and **p** are integers, this result is a multiple of 12 (as it is "12 × an integer")  *

> *Think how this result can be a multiple of 24 (for example 12 × 2, or "12 × even number" )*

*to be a multiple of 24, either (***n*** - ***p***) must be even or 3(***n*** + ***p***) + 1 must be even*

**[1]**

> *Remember "odd - odd = even", "even - even = even", "odd + even = odd", "even + odd = odd" *

> *By considering **n** and **p** being odd and even, prove the statement above*

*if ***n*** is odd and ***p*** is odd, then ***n*** - ***p*** is even*
* **if ***n*** is even and ***p*** is even, then ***n*** - ***p*** is even** *
*if ***n*** is odd and ***p*** is even, then ***n*** +*** p*** is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) + 1 is even** *
*if ***n*** is even and ***p*** is odd, then*** n*** + ***p*** is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) + 1 is even**  *

**In all cases of ****n**** and ****p**** being odd and even, either (****n**** - ****p****) is even or 3(****n**** + ****p****) + 1 is even so **`equation`** is a multiple of 24 ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Prove that , for all positive values of $n$,

$\frac{\left(n  + 2 \right)^{2}  -  \left(n  + 1\right)^{2}}{2 n^{2}  +  3 n}  =  \frac{1}{n}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Expand (**n** + 2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* * * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 2\right)^{2} & = & \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 2\right) \\ & = & n^{2} + 2 n + 2 n + 4 \\ & = & n^{2} + 4 n + 4\end{aligned}$ * *

*Expand (**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* * * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 1\right)^{2} & = & \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) \\ & = & n^{2} + n + n + 1 \\ & = & n^{2} + 2 n + 1 \\ & & \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Put these results in brackets and subtract the second from the first* * *

$\left(n + 2\right)^{2} - \left(n + 1\right)^{2} = \left(n^{2} + 4 n + 4\right) - \left(n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side * *Collect "like" terms* * *

$n^{2}+4n+4-n^{2}-2n-1\,=2n+3$

**[1]**

*Write the algebraic fraction with the numerator as 2**n** + 3* * *

$\frac{2n+3}{2n^{2}+3n}$* *

> *Factorise the denominator (by taking out a factor of **n**)  *

$\frac{2 n + 3}{n \left(2 n + 3\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Cancel the (2**n** + 3) bracket from top-and-bottom  *

> $\frac{\cancel{2 n + 3}}{n \cancel{\left(2 n + 3\right)}} = \frac{1}{n}$*  *

$\frac{1}{n}$** ****[1]**

*Method 2*

*The "difference of two squares" says **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2 *</sup>*= (**a **+ **b**)(**a** - **b**) Factorise (**n** + 2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - (**n** + 1)*<sup>*2 *</sup>*using the "difference of two squares" where** a** = **n** + 2 and **b** = **n** + 1* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 2\right)^{2} - \left(n + 1\right)^{2} & = & \left(\left(n + 2\right) + \left(n + 1\right)\right) \times \left(\left(n + 2\right) + \left(n + 1\right)\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the brackets on the right-hand side * * *

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(n + 2 + n + 1\right) \left(n + 2 - n - 1\right) \\ & = & \left(2 n + 3\right) \left(1\right) \\ & = & 2 n + 3\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Write the algebraic fraction with the numerator as 2**n** + 3* * *

$\frac{2n+3}{2n^{2}+3n}$* *

> *Factorise the denominator   *

$\frac{2 n + 3}{n \left(2 n + 3\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Cancel the (2**n** + 3) bracket from top-and-bottom  *

> $\frac{\cancel{2 n + 3}}{n \cancel{\left(2 n + 3\right)}} = \frac{1}{n}$*  *

$\frac{1}{n}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$N$ is a multiple of 5

$\begin{aligned}A  & = &  N  +  1 \\ B  & = &  N  –  1\end{aligned}$

Prove, using algebra, that $A^{2}--B^{2}$ is always a multiple of 20
parts.solutionMd:
> *As *$N$* is a multiple of 5,*

*Let *$N=5k$*, were *$k$* is an integer*

> *Rewrite *$A$* and *$B$* in terms of *$k$*.*

parts.problemMd:
Expressions for consecutive triangular numbers are

$\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}$ and $\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2}$

Prove that the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is always a square number.
parts.solutionMd:
*Do not be put off by the fractions!* *They already have a common denominator so we can write their sum as a single fraction.*

$\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2} + \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2} = \frac{n \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2}$

*Expand and simplify the numerator.* *If you spot it, the numerator has a factor of (**n** + 1) which can make simplifying easier.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2} & = & \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + \left(n + 2\right)\right)}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + \left(n + 2\right)\right)}{2} & = & \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *There is a factor of 2 in the second bracket on the numerator that will then cancel with the denominator.*

$\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)}{2} = \frac{\cancel{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right)}{\cancel{2}}$

> *We are left with the product of two equal brackets.*

$\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) = \left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

> *This is the form **k*<sup>*2*</sup>*, for an integer **k** (assuming **n** is an integer) and so is a square number.*

**Since the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers can be written in the form (****n**** + 1)**<sup>**2**</sup>**, for integer ****n****, it is always a square number** **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:

> *Working through each statement in turn, starting with the left hand side and comparing it to the right hand side.*

$\begin{aligned}LHS & = & x + 4 x \\ & = & 5 x \\ & = & RHS\end{aligned}$

> *Therefore this is true for **all** values of x and this is the answer.*

**The correct identity is the first option, **$x+4x\equiv5x$** as this is the only statement that is true for all values of x ****[1]**

> *When using a 'test each option' approach such as this, particularly when the first option 'works', *

> *it is a good idea to check the other options too to check.*

> $6x=18$* is only true when *$x=3$* so is not true for all values of **x** (it's an equation). *

> $2x+1=7,2x=6$* is only true when *$x=3$* so is not true for all values of **x** (it's an equation). *

> $7x+9=x,6x=-9$* is only true when *$x=-1.5$* so is not true for all values of x (it's an equation).*

> *Now find **L** - **T**.*

**L*** - ***T*** = 1224 - 1125 = 99*

**L**** - ****T**** = 99*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Prove that, for any position of the cross on the number grid above, $L--T=99.$
parts.solutionMd:
> *(We may assume that **M** only takes values that means the cross can be drawn on the grid.  So **M** ≠ 30 for example.)*

> *For middle value **M*

*the left and right numbers of the cross will be (***M*** - 1) and (***M*** + 1)* *∴ ***L*** = (***M*** - 1)(***M*** + 1)*

**[1]**

*the top and bottom numbers of the cross will be (M - 10) and (M + 10)* *∴ ***T*** = (***M*** - 10)(***M*** + 10)*

**[1]**

> *So*

$L - T = \left(M - 1\right) \left(M + 1\right) - \left(M - 10\right) \left(M + 10\right)$

> *Expand each pair of brackets, being careful with the subtraction sign between them. Both brackets are in the difference of two squares form.*

$L - T = \left(M^{2} - 1\right) - \left(M^{2} - 100\right)$

**For (M**<sup>**2**</sup>** -1)**** [1] **
**For (M**<sup>**2**</sup>** -100)**** [1]**

> *Remove the brackets and simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}L - T & = & M^{2} - 1 - M^{2} + 100 \\ & = & 100 - 1 \\ & = & 99\end{aligned}$

$\thereforeL-T=99$* ***for any position of the cross on the number grid*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$c$ is a positive integer.

Prove that  $\frac{6c^{3}+30c}{3c^{2}+15}$  is an even number.
parts.solutionMd:
> *An even number can be written in the form 2**k**, where **k** is an integer.*

> *To do this we would look to factorise the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors.*

$\frac{6 c^{3} + 30 c}{3 c^{2} + 15} = \frac{6 c \left(c^{2} + 5\right)}{3 \left(c^{2} + 5\right)}$

**Correctly factorsing numerator or denominator ****[1]**** **
**Correctly factorsing both ****[1]**

> *There are factors of 3 and *$\left(c^{2} + 5\right)$* that can be cancelled.*

$\frac{\begin{matrix}2 c \left(c^{2} + 5\right) \\ \cancel{6} c \bcancel{\left(c^{2} + 5\right)}\end{matrix}}{\cancel{3} \bcancel{\left(c^{2} + 5\right)}} = 2 c$

> *We can now conclude the proof.*

**Since **$\frac{6c^{3}+30c}{3c^{2}+15}=2c$** and c is an integer, it is a multiple of 2 and so must be an even number** **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Prove that the mean of any four consecutive even integers is an integer.
parts.solutionMd:
*Write down an algebraic expression for an even integer.*

> *By letting an integer be **n**, then we can be sure it will be even by multiplying it by 2.*

*Let ***n ***be an integer, then 2***n ***is an even integer** *

**[1]**

> *Write down the algebraic expression for the next three consecutive even numbers after 2**n **(adding 2 each time).*

*2***n*** + 2 *
*2***n*** + 4 *
*2***n*** + 6*

> *Write down an expression showing the mean of the four consecutive even numbers by adding them together and dividing by 4.*

$\frac{2n+2n+2+2n+4+2n+6}{4}$

**Adding the terms together ****[1]**

*SImplify the numerator by collecting like terms.* * *

$\frac{2n+2n+2n+2n+2+4+6}{4}=\frac{8n+12}{4}$

**Simplifying and dividing by 4 ****[1]*** *

> *Factorise the numerator.*

$\frac{4 \left(2 n + 3\right)}{4}$

> *Cancel 4 from the numerator and denominator.*

$\frac{\cancel{4} \left(2 n + 3\right)}{\cancel{4}} = 2 n + 3$

*As **n** was an integer**,** 2**n **+ 3 must also be an integer. *

**The mean of any four consecutive even integers is an integer because 2****n ****+ 3 is an integer for any integer ****n. ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: The lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle are all integers. Prove that if the lengths of the two shortest sides are even, then the length of the third side must also be even.
parts.solutionMd:
*Pythagoras' theorem links the three sides, **a**, **b** and **c** of a right angled triangle.* *If **a** is the longest side, the hypotenuse, then *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}$*.*

> *Start by introducing the two shorter sides as even values.*

*Let the two shorter sides be 2***m*** and 2***n***, where ***m*** and ***n*** are integers*

> *Apply Pythagoras' theorem, where these two sides/values would be **b** and **c*

$a^{2} = \left(2 m\right)^{2} + \left(2 n\right)^{2}$

> *Expand the right-hand side.*

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} & = & 4 m^{2} + 4 n^{2} \\ a^{2} & = & 4 \left(m^{2} + n^{2}\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Since we are given all three sides are integers, we can assume that *$4 \left(m^{2} + n^{2}\right)$* is a square number.*

**a***<sup>2</sup>** has a factor of 4, which is even and so ***a***<sup>2</sup>** is even*

*if a square number is even, its (positive) square root is even ***a***<sup>2</sup>** is even, therefore ***a*** is even*

**Therefore if the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with integer sides are even, the third side is even too ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Prove that the sum of four consecutive whole numbers is always even.
parts.solutionMd:
> *An even number can be written in the form 2**k**, where **k** is an integer.*

> *Start by introducing the four consecutive whole numbers.*

*Let ***n*** be the lowest of the four consecutive whole numbers* *The other three will then be ***n*** + 1, ***n*** + 2 and ***n*** + 3*

**[1]**

> *Add these together and simplify the result.*

$\begin{aligned}n + \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 2\right) + \left(n + 3\right) & = & 4 n + 6 \\ & = & 2 \left(2 n + 3\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This is in the form 2**k** so we can conclude the proof.*

**Since ****n**** is a whole number (integer), 2****n**** + 3 is an integer and so 2(2****n**** + 3) is in the form 2****k****, where ****k**** is an integer and so the sum of four consecutive whole numbers is always even**** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Give an example to show that the sum of four consecutive integers is **not** always divisible by 4.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Only one example is needed to disprove a statement so try some numbers until you find a set that show the desired result, rather than trying to use algebra.*

*Try the four consecutive integers 1, 2, 3 and 4*

*1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10*

**[1]**

*10 is not divisible by 4*

**1, 2, 3 and 4 are four consecutive integers whose sum (10) is not divisible by 4** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Express as a single fraction.

$\frac{m+1}{n+1}-\frac{m}{n}$

Simplify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the lowest common denominator (lcd) by multiplying (**n** + 1) by **n**.*

*lcd is (***n*** + 1) × ***n*** = ***n***(***n*** + 1)*

> *Multiply numerator-and-denominator of each fraction by the factor needed to form this denominator.*

$\frac{\left(m + 1\right) n}{n \left(n + 1\right)} - \frac{m \left(n + 1\right)}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Write as one single fraction over the common denominator. Subtract the numerators.*

$\frac{n \left(m + 1\right) - m \left(n + 1\right)}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets in the numerator.*

$\frac{m n + n - m n - m}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Collect "like" terms in the numerator.*

$\frac{n - m}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Nothing else factorises or cancels.*

$\therefore\frac{m+1}{n+1}-\frac{m}{n}=\frac{n-m}{n(n+1)}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Using your answer to part (**a**), prove that if m and n are positive integers and $m<n$, then

$\frac{m+1}{n+1}-\frac{m}{n}>0$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The result from part (a) is that*

$\frac{m + 1}{n + 1} - \frac{m}{n} = \frac{n - m}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Consider the numerator.*

$n-m>0$* since ***n*** > ***m*** and both ***n*** and ***m*** are positive*

**[1]**

> *Consider the denominator.*

$n \left(n + 1\right) > 0$* since ***n*** is positive (and *$n+1>n$* )*

> *So both the numerator and denominator are positive.*

*A positive number divided by a positive number is positive*

$\therefore\frac{m+1}{n+1}-\frac{m}{n}=\frac{n-m}{n(n+1)}>0$** if ****m**** and ****n**** are positve integers and ****m**** < ****n ****since both **$(n-m)$** and **$n(n+1)$** are positive ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Prove algebraically that the difference between the squares of any two consecutive odd numbers is always a multiple of 8
parts.solutionMd:
> *Define expressions for consecutive odd numbers*

*Let *$n$* equal any integer*

*Therefore *$2n+1$* equals any odd number*

*And *$2n+3$* equals the next consecutive odd number*

**[M1]**

> *Use your expressions to set up an expression to show the difference between the squares of consecutive odd numbers*

$\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n + 1\right)^{2}$

> *Expand the brackets, using FOIL method for example*

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n + 1\right)^{2} & = & \left(4 n^{2} + 6 n + 6 n + 9\right) - \left(4 n^{2} + 2 n + 2 n + 1\right)\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Simplify the expression by collecting terms*

$\begin{aligned} & = & \left(4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9\right) - \left(4 n^{2} + 4 n + 1\right) \\ & = & 4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9 - 4 n^{2} - 4 n - 1 \\ & = & 8 n + 8\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Factorise the simplified expression by dividing the expression by the highest common factor of the terms*

**Final answer:** $8 n + 8 = 8 \left(n + 1\right)$** therefore it is a multiple of 8**

**[A1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Form an expression for the area of the rectangle.*

$\begin{aligned}A_{r e c t} & = & length \times width = \left(3 x - 2\right) \left(x - 1\right) \end{aligned}$

> *Form an expression for the area of the triangle using the formula *$A=\frac{1}{2}bh$*. *

$\begin{aligned}A_{t r i} & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(x\right) \left(2 x\right)\end{aligned}$

**Both expressions formed **** [1]**

> *Form an **inequality **by setting the expression for the area of the rectangle **greater than **the expression for the area of the triangle.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(3 x - 2\right) \left(x - 1\right) & > & \frac{1}{2} \left(x\right) \left(2 x\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the left-hand side by expanding the double brackets and collecting the like terms together.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} - 3 x - 2 x + 2 & > & \frac{1}{2} \left(x\right) \left(2 x\right) \\ 3 x^{2} - 5 x + 2 & > & \frac{1}{2} \left(x\right) \left(2 x\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the right-hand side by cancelling the 2s.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} - 5 x + 2 & > & \frac{1}{\cancel{2}} \left(x\right) \left(\cancel{2} x\right) \\ 3 x^{2} - 5 x + 2 & > & x^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange to make this a quadratic equation equal to zero.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} - 5 x + 2 - x^{2} & > & 0 \\ 2 x^{2} - 5 x + 2 & > & 0\end{aligned}$

** **** [1]**

> *Begin to factorise by multiplying 2 by 2.*

*2 × 2 = 4*

> *Find two numbers that multiply to give 4 and add to give -5 (the middle number)*

*-1 and -4*

$2x^{2}-x-4x+2>0$

> *Factorise fully the first pair of terms and the second pair of terms, either 2 or -2 could be factorised out of the last two terms, but the aim is to get the brackets the same so -2 should be factorised. *

$x \left(2 x - 1\right) - 2 \left(2 x - 1\right) > 0$

> *Factorise out the whole (2**x** - 1) bracket as if it were one term, leaving **x **and -2 in their own bracket.*

$\left(x - 2\right) \left(2 x - 1\right) > 0$

** **** [1]**

> *This means that the graph of *$y=2x^{2}-5x+2$* has roots at *$x=2$* and *$x=\frac{1}{2}$*.*

> *We are interested in the region where **y** is greater than 0, so this will be where the graph is above the **x-**axis. *

> *As the quadratic is positive, this will be in the regions above and below the roots.*

> * *$x>2\mathrm{and}x<\frac{1}{2}$

**allowing sign errors**** [1]**

> *Considering the expressions given for the length and width of the rectangle, we can find restrictions on the value of **x. **Remember that both the length and the width must be positive.*

$l = 3 x - 2 \Leftrightarrow x > \frac{ 2 }{3} ( \text{as} l > 0 )$
$w = x - 1 \Leftrightarrow x > 1 ( \text{as} w > 0 )$

> *As *$x>1$*, disregard *$x<\frac{1}{2}$*.*

$x>2$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
3 kg of potatoes and 4 kg of carrots have a total cost of 440p. 
4 kg of potatoes and 3 kg of carrots have a total cost of 470p.

Work out the total cost of 1 kg of potatoes and 1 kg of carrots.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Let potatoes be **p** and carrots be **c. *

> *Use the information in the question to write two equations:*

> *3 kg of potatoes = 3**p, **4 kg of carrots = 4**c *

$3p+4c=440$

> *4 kg of potatoes = 4**p, **3 kg of carrots = 3**c *

$4p+3c=470$

> *Number the equations.*

> $\begin{aligned}3 p + 4 c & = & 440 \left(1\right) \\ 4 p + 3 c & = & 470 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *This is a non calculator paper so the easiest method is to spot that adding the two equations will give and equal number of potatoes and carrots.*

> *The questions asks for the price of 1 kg of potatoes and 1 kg of carrots, so there is no need to find their individual prices.*

> *Add equation (1) to equation (2).*

$\begin{matrix} 3 p + 4 c = 440 \\ \underline{+ \left(4 p + 3 c = 470 \right)} \\ 7 p + 7 c = 910 \end{matrix}$

**[1]**

> *This gives the cost of 7 kg of potatoes and 7 kg of carrots. *

> *Find the cost of 1 kg of each by dividing by 7.*

space space 7 p space plus space 7 c space equals space 910 space
$7 ( p + c ) = 910$
$p + c = \frac{ 910}{7}$

**[1]**

> *This finds the total cost of 1 kg of carrots and 1 kg of potatoes.*

$p+c=130p$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Let potatoes be **p** and carrots be **c. *

> *Use the information in the question to write two equations:*

> *3 kg of potatoes = 3**p, **4 kg of carrots = 4**c *

$3p+4c=440$

> *4 kg of potatoes = 4**p, **3 kg of carrots = 3**c *

$4p+3c=470$

> *Number the equations.*

> $\begin{aligned}3 p + 4 c & = & 440 \left(1\right) \\ 4 p + 3 c & = & 470 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *Make the **p** terms equal by multiplying all parts of equation (1) by 4 and all parts of equation (2) by 3.*

> $\begin{aligned} & & 4 \left(1\right) 4 \left(3 p + 4 c = 440\right) \\ & & 3 \left(2\right) 3 \left(4 p + 3 c = 470\right) \end{aligned}$*  *

> *This gives the two new equations:*

$\begin{aligned}12 p + 16 c & = & 1760 \left(3\right) \\ 12 p + 9 c & = & 1410 \left(4\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Eliminate the **p** terms by subtracting equation (4) from equation (3).*

$\begin{array}{r} 12 p + 16 c = 1760 \\ \underline{ - \left(12 p + 9 c = 1410\right) } \\ 7 c = 350 \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation to find** c  **by dividing both sides by 7.*

$\begin{aligned}c & = & \frac{350}{7} = 50\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$c=50$* into either of the two original equations**.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(2\right) 3 p + 4 c & = & 440 \\ 3 p + 4 \left(50\right) & = & 440 \\ 3 p + 200 & = & 440\end{aligned}$

> *Solve this equation to find** p.*

$\begin{aligned}3 p + 200 & = & 440 \\ 3 p & = & 240 \\ p & = & \frac{240}{3} = 80 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This means that 1 kg of carrots is 50p and 1 kg of potatoes is 80p.*

> *Add them together to get the total.*

$p+c=130p$* ***[1]**

$3a+c=30$

> *1 adult ticket = **a, **3 child tickets = 3**c,** add these and set equal to 22. *

$a+3c=22$

> *Number the equations.*

> $\begin{aligned}3 a + c & = & 30 \left(1\right) \\ a + 3 c & = & 22 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *

> *Make the **c** terms equal by multiplying all parts of equation (1) by 3.*

> $3 ( 1 ) 3 ( 3 a + c = 30 )$
$( 2 ) a + 3 c = 22$*  *

> *This gives the two equation with the same coefficient of **c.*

$\begin{aligned}9 a + 3 c & = & 90 \left(3\right) \\ a + 3 c & = & 22 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Eliminate the **c** terms by subtracting equation (2) from equation (3).*

$\begin{gathered} 9 \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} a \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} + \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} 3 \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} c \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} = \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} 90 \end{gathered}$
$\underline{-\ (a + 3c = 22)}$

> *Solve the equation to find** a  **by dividing both sides by 8.*

$\begin{aligned}a & = & \frac{68}{8} = 8 . 5\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\left(1\right) 3 a + c & = & 30 \\ 3 \left(8 . 5\right) + c & = & 30 \\ 25 . 5 + c & = & 30\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve this equation to find** c.*

$\begin{aligned}c + 25 . 5 & = & 30 \\ c & = & 30 - 25 . 5 \\ c & = & 4 . 5 \end{aligned}$

> *This means that 1 adult ticket costs £8.50 and 1 child ticket costs £4.50. *

**Adult ticket = £8.50 **

![q7-meduim-2-13-forming-and-solving-equations-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/algebra-and-sequences/forming-and-solving-equations/assets/020-q7-meduim-2-13-forming-and-solving-equations-ede.png)

The diagram shows a parallelogram.

The sizes of the angles, in degrees, are

$2x\,3x-15\,2x\,2x+24$

Work out the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360*<sup>*o*</sup>*.*

*Write down an equation adding together all four angles.*

$2x+2x+(3x-15)+(2x+24)=360$

> *You can rewrite the equation without brackets.*

$2x+2x+3x-15+2x+24=360$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange the equation so that like terms are next to each other, remember to keep the sign in front of each term the same as it was when you re-arrange. *

$2x+2x+3x+2x-15+24=360$

> *Add/subtract the like terms, being careful with negatives!*

$9x+9=360$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation. *

> *It may be easiest to factorise the 9 out first.*

$\begin{aligned}9 x + 9 & = & 360 \\ 9 \left(x + 1\right) & = & 360 \\ x + 1 & = & \frac{ 360}{9} \\ x + 1 & = & 40 \\ x & = & 39\end{aligned}$

$x=39^{\circ}$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal.*

> *Write down an equation for the two opposite angles that have **different **expressions.*

$3x-15=2x+24$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation by first bringing the **x** terms to one side. *

> * The easiest method is to subtract the **x** term with the smallest coefficient.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x - 15 & = & 2 x + 24 \\ - 2 x & = & - 2 x \\ x - 15 & = & 24\end{aligned}$

> *Add 15 to both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}x - 15 & = & 24 \\ + 15 & = & + 15 \\ x & = & 39 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$x=39^{\circ}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
3 teas and 2 coffees have a total cost of £7.80

Work out the cost of one tea and the cost of one coffee.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Let the cost of a tea be **t** and the cost of a coffee be **c. *

> *Use the information in the question to write two equations.*

> *3 teas = 3**t, **2 coffees = 2**c,** add these and set equal to 7.8 (£7.80). *

$3t+2c=7.8$

> *5 teas = 5**t, **4 coffees = 4**c,** add these and set equal to 14.2 (£14.20). *

$5t+4c=14.2$

**[1]**

> *Number the equations.*

> $\begin{aligned}3 t + 2 c & = & 7 . 8 \left(1\right) \\ 5 t + 4 c & = & 14 . 2 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *

> *Make the **c** terms equal by multiplying all parts of equation (1) by 2.*

$2 ( 1 ) 2 ( 3 t + 2 c = 7.8 )$
$( 2 ) \begin{array}{rcl} \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} 5 \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} t \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} + \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} 4 \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} c \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} = \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} 14 \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} . \end{array} \begin{array}{rcl} 2 \end{array}$*  *

> *This gives two equations with the same coefficient of **c.*

$\begin{aligned}6 t + 4 c & = & 15 . 6 \left(3\right) \\ 5 t + 4 c & = & 14 . 2 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Eliminate the **c** terms by subtracting equation (2) from equation (3).*

$\begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} 6 \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} t \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} + \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} 4 \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} c \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} = \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} 15 \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} . \end{gathered} \begin{gathered} 6 \end{gathered}$
$\underline{-\ (5t + 4c = 14.2)}$
$t = 1.4$

**[1]**

> *Substitute *$t=1.4$* into either of the two original equations**.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(1\right) 3 t + 2 c & = & 7 . 8 \\ 3 \left(1 . 4\right) + 2 c & = & 7 . 8 \\ 4 . 2 + 2 c & = & 7 . 8\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve this equation to find** c.*

$\begin{aligned}2 c & = & 7 . 8 - 4 . 2 \\ 2 c & = & 3 . 6 \\ c & = & \frac{3 . 6}{2} = 1 . 8\end{aligned}$

> *This means that 1 tea costs £1.40 and 1 coffee costs £1.80. *

**One tea = £1.40    **
**   One coffee = £1.80 ****[1]**

All measurements are in metres. 
The perimeter of the garden is 32 metres.

Work out the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The perimeter of a shape is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For a rectangle this is length + width + length + width, or 2(length + width).*

> *Use this to form an expression for the perimeter of the rectangle.*

$\begin{aligned}P & = & l + w + l + w \\ P & = & 2 l + 2 w \\ & = & 2 \left(4 + 3 x\right) + 2 \left(x + 6\right) \end{aligned}$

** **** [1]**

> *Form an equation for the perimeter of the rectangle, setting it equal to 32 metres.*

$\begin{aligned}Perimeter & = & 32 \\ 2 \left(4 + 3 x\right) + 2 \left(x + 6\right) & = & 32\end{aligned}$

** **** [1]**

> *Simplify by first expanding the brackets and collecting the like terms.*

$\begin{aligned}2 \left(4 + 3 x\right) + 2 \left(x + 6\right) & = & 32 \\ 8 + 6 x + 2 x + 12 & = & 32 \\ 8 x + 20 & = & 32\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the equation to find *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}8 x + 20 & = & 32 \\ - 20 & = & - 20 \\ 8 x & = & 12 \\ \div 8 & = & \div 8 \\ x & = & \frac{12}{8} \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$x=1.5$**  ****[1]**

All the measurements are in centimetres.

The area of the trapezium is 351 cm<sup>2</sup>.

Show that  $2x^{2}+x---351=0$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute the values in the diagram into the formula for the area of a trapezium. *

> *The formula is *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the two parallel sides and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$A = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(\left(x - 4\right) + \left(x + 5\right)\right) \times 2 x$

**[1]**

> *The area is given as 351 cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*, so set this expression equal to 351.*

$\frac{1}{2} \times \left(\left(x - 4\right) + \left(x + 5\right)\right) \times 2 x = 351$

> *Simplify the expression in the brackets.*

$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} \times \left(2 x + 1\right) \times 2 x & = & 351\end{aligned}$

> *Cancel out the 2.*

$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\cancel{2}} \times \left(2 x + 1\right) \times \cancel{2} x & = & 351 \\ x \left(2 x + 1\right) & = & 351\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets on the right hand side.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x^{2} + x & = & 351\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 351 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x^{2} + x - 351 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

$2x^{2}+x-351=0$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Work out the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute the given values into the quadratic formula*

> *Given an equation of the form *$ax^{2}+bx+c=0$*, the quadratic formula is *$x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$*.*

> *Identify the values of **a, b **and **c.*

$a=2,b=1,c=-351$

> *Substitute into the quadratic formula.*

$x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1^{2}-4\times2\times-351}}{2\times2}$

** [1]**

> *Simplify the right hand side.*

$x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{2809}}{4}$

** [1]**

> *Work out the two results by doing the calculation twice, once using the positive sign and once using the negative sign in front of the square root.*

$x=13$* or *$x=-13.5$

> *Considering the diagram in part (a), the height of the trapezium is *$2x$*, so *$x$* must be positive.*

** **$x=13$** ****[1]**

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}2 \left(5\right) + 6 & = & 16 or 5 \left(5\right) - 9 = 16\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Area = length × width. We have a length of 16, a width of *$y$*, and the area is 48, so*

$\begin{aligned}16 y & = & 48 \\ y & = & \frac{48}{16} = 3\end{aligned}$

$y=3$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
In a chess club, there are $x$ boys and $y$ girls.

If 5 more boys and 8 more girls join, there would be half as many boys as girls.

Show that $y=2x+2$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *If 5 more boys and 8 more girls join there will be *

$x+5$* **boys and *$y+8$* girls*

> *If there are half as many boys as girls then;*

$x + 5 = \frac{1}{2} \left(y + 8\right)$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 2 to clear the fraction.*

$2x+10=y+8$

> *And subtract 8 from both sides.*

$2x+2=y$** [1]**

> *Method 2*

> *If 5 more boys and 8 more girls join there will be *

$x+5$* **boys and *$y+8$* girls*

> *If there are half as many boys as girls then;*

$2 \left(x + 5\right) = y + 8$

**[1]**

> *Expand the bracket.*

$2x+10=y+8$

> *And subtract 8 from both sides.*

$2x+2=y$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
If instead,

10 more boys and 1 more girl join, there would be the same number of boys and girls.

Work out $x$ and $y$.

$x$ = ...................

$y$ = ...................
parts.solutionMd:
> *If 10 more boys and 1 more girls join there will be;*

*'*$x+10$*' boys and '*$y+1$*' girls*

> *The number of boys equals the number of girls.*

$x+10=y+1$

**[1]**

> *Subtract one from both sides.*

$x+9=y$

> *If we combine this with the equation given in part (a), then we have a pair of simultaneous equations.*

$y=x+9\mathrm{and}y=2x+2$

> *We can solve these by elimination or substitution. Here we will use substitution.*

$x+9=2x+2$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}x + 9 & = & 2 x + 2 \\ - x & = & - x \\ 9 & = & x + 2 \\ - 2 & = & - 2 \\ 7 & = & x\end{aligned}$

> *Solve, in this case by subtracting  *$\begin{aligned} & & x\end{aligned}$* and then subtracting 2 from both sides.*

$x=7$** [1]**

> *Be careful! We have not fully answered the question until we have found *$\begin{aligned} & & y\end{aligned}$*. Substitute *$\begin{aligned}x & = & 7\end{aligned}$* into *$\begin{aligned}y & = & x + 9\end{aligned}$* or *$\begin{aligned}y & = & 2 x + 2\end{aligned}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 7 + 9 = 16 or y = 2 \left(7\right) + 2 = 16\end{aligned}$

$y=16$* ***[1]**

**Perform a mental check; "7 boys and 10 more join means 17 boys; 16 girls and one more joins means 17 girls; the same number of boys and girls" **

parts.problemMd:
Ali is $y$ years old.

Bhavara is twice as old as Ali.

Ceris is 3 years younger than Ali.

The total of their ages is 125 years.

Work out the age of each person.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Let Ali, **A**, by **y  **years old and use this to write expressions for the ages of Bhavara, **B**, and Ceris, **C. *

$A=y\,B=2y\,C=y-3$

**[1]**

> *The word total means 'the sum of', so add the expressions together and form an equation by setting this equal to 125.*

$\begin{aligned}A + B + C & = & 125 \\ y + 2 y + \left(y - 3\right) & = & 125 \\ 4 y - 3 & = & 125\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now solve the equation to find *$y$*.*

$\begin{aligned}4 y - 3 & = & 125 \\ + 3 & = & + 3 \\ 4 y & = & 128 \\ \div 4 & = & \div 4 \\ y & = & \frac{128}{4} \\ & = & 32\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> $y=32$* means that Ali is 32 years old.  *

> *Now substitute *$y=32$* into the expressions for **B **and **C.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & y = 32 \\ B & = & 2 y = 2 \left(32\right) \\ C & = & y - 3 = 32 - 3\end{aligned}$

**Ali: 32 years       **
** ****Bhavara: 64 years    **
**  **** ****Ceris: 29 years****  ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Theo starts with savings of £18

James starts with no savings.

Each week from now,

Theo will save £4.50 and James will save £4

In how many weeks will Theo and James have savings in the ratio 15 : 8 ?
parts.solutionMd:
> *You could do this by trial and error, adding £4.50 and £4 to their respective totals over and over and checking each time whether the ratio has become 15 : 8. *

> *That could take a long time, however, so it's better to use a more algebraic approach.*

> *Call the number of weeks from the start "**N **". Then write a formula in terms of **N** for how much they each have after **N** weeks.*

$\mathrm{Theo}:18+4.5N\,\,\mathrm{James}:4N$

**[1]**

> *Next turn the ratio we are looking for into an equation with the expressions for James' and Theo's money. *

> *Begin solving the equation.*

$\frac{Theo}{James} = \frac{18 + 4.5 N}{4 N} = \frac{15}{8}$

$8 \times ( 18 + 4.5 N ) = 15 \times 4 N$

144 space plus space 36 N space equals space 60 space N

**[1]**

> *Finish solving the equation to find the value of **N**.*

$144=60N-36N\,\,144=24N\,\,N=144\div24=6$

**Final answer:** **6 weeks****  [1]**

$\begin{aligned}x + 4 x + 40 + 5 x + 40 & = & 360 \\ 10 x + 80 & = & 360\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd:
Rana sells 192 cakes in the ratio    small : medium : large    =    7 : 6 : 11

The profit for one medium cake is twice the profit for one small cake. 
The profit for one large cake is three times the profit for one small cake.

Her total profit is £532.48

Work out the profit for one small cake.

£.....................
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by working out how many of each size cake she makes. Add up the ratio numbers to find the number of 'parts' that the 192 cakes are divided into.*

> * Then divide 192 by that sum to find the size of one part.*

$7+6+11=24\,\,192\div24=8$

**[1]**

> *So one part is 8 cakes. *

> *To find the amount of each size of cake, multiply 8 by the respective ratio numbers.*

$\mathrm{small}:8\times7=56\,\,\mathrm{medium}:8\times6=48\,\,\mathrm{large}:8\times11=88$

**[1]**

> *Call the profit for one small cake "**x** ". *

> *Then the profit for a medium cake is 2**x**, and the profit for a large cake is 3**x. *

> *Use this and the numbers of cakes from above to set up an equation equal to the total profit. *

> *Begin to solve the equation.*

$( 56 \times x ) + ( 48 \times 2 x ) + ( 88 \times 3 x ) = 532.48$

56 x space plus space 96 x space plus 264 x space equals space 532.48

416 x space equals space 532.48

**[1] **
**The mark here is for setting up a correct equation.**

> *Finish solving the equation to find the value of **x**  (which is also the profit for one small cake).*

$x=532.48\div416=1.28$

**[1]**

**£1.28****  [1]**

 The ratio of Sundip’s money to Emma’s money is now 2 : 3.

**[2] **

parts.problemMd:
Make $y$ the subject of the formula

$t=\frac{2-3y}{y+2}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove the fraction (by multiplying both sides by **y** + 2)* * *

$t \left(y + 2\right) = 2 - 3 y$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying the terms inside by **t**)* * *

$ty+2t=2-3y$ * *

*Collect the **y** terms on one side (for example, by adding 3**y** to both sides then subtracting 2**t **from both sides)* * *

$\begin{aligned}t y + 2 t + 3 y & = & 2 \\ t y + 3 y & = & 2 - 2 t\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise** y** out of the terms on the left* * *

$y \left(t + 3\right) = 2 - 2 t$

**[1]**

*Get y on its own (by dividing both sides by **t** + 3)* * *

$y=\frac{2-2t}{t+3}$* ***[1]**

$y=\frac{2t-2}{-t-3}$** is also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $y$ the subject of the formula    $p=\sqrt{\frac{x+y}{5}}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove the square-root sign (by squaring both sides)* * *

$p^{2}=\frac{x+y}{5}$

**[1]**

*Get **x** + **y** on its own (by multiplying both sides by 5)* * *

$5p^{2}=x+y$

**[1]**

*Get **y** on its own (by subtracting **x** from both sides)* * *

$5p^{2}-x=y$

$y=5p^{2}-x$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Make $v$ the subject of the formula $w  =  \frac{15 \left(t  -  2 v\right)}{v}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove fractions (by multiplying both sides by **v**)* * *

$w v = 15 \left(t - 2 v\right)$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying the terms inside by 15)* * *

$wv=15t-30v$ * *

*Move the **v** terms to one side (for example, by adding 30**v** to both sides)* * *

$wv+30v=15t$ * *

*Factorise **v** out of the terms on the left* * *

$v \left(w + 30\right) = 15 t$

**[1]**

> *Get **v** on its own (by dividing both sides by **w** + 30)*

$v=\frac{15t}{w+30}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Make $t$the subject of the formula   $2 \left(d - t\right)  =  4 t  + 7$

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying the terms inside by 2)* * *

$2d-2t=4t+7$ * *

*Get the **t** terms on one side (for example, by adding 2**t** to both sides and collecting "like" terms)* * *

$2d=4t+7+2t\,2d=6t+7$

**[1]**

*Get 6**t** on its own (by subtracting 7 from both sides)* * *

$2d-7=6t$

**[1]**

*Get **t** on its own (by dividing both sides by 6)* * *

$\frac{2d-7}{6}=t$

$t=\frac{2d-7}{6}$* ***[1]**

$t=\frac{7-2d}{-6}$** is also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $t$ the subject of the formula $w=3t+11$

**[1]**

> *Get **t** on its own (by dividing both sides by 3)  *

$t=\frac{w-11}{3}$**[1]**

parts.problemMd: Make $a$ the subject of       $a+3=\frac{2a+7}{r}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove fractions (by multiplying both sides by **r**)* * *

$r \left(a + 3\right) = 2 a + 7$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying the terms inside by **r**)* * *

$ra+3r=2a+7$ * *

*Move the **a** terms to one side (for example, by subtracting 2**a** from both sides)* * *

$ra+3r-2a=7$ * *

*Get the **a** terms on their own (by subtracting 3**r** from both sides)* * *

$ra-2a=7-3r$ * *

*Factorise **a** out of the terms on the left* * *

$a \left(r - 2\right) = 7 - 3 r$

**[1]**

> *Get **a** on its own (by dividing both sides by **r **- 2)*

$a=\frac{7-3r}{r-2}$* ***[1]**

$a=\frac{3r-7}{2-r}$** is also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $m$ the subject of the formula      $v=\sqrt{\frac{2E}{m}}$

parts.problemMd: Make $F$ the subject of the formula  $C  =  \frac{5 \left(F  -  32\right)}{9}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Get 5(**F** - 32) on its own (by multiplying both sides by 9)* * *

$9 C = 5 \left(F - 32\right)$

**[1]**

*Method 1*

*Get **F** - 32 on its own (by dividing both sides by 5)* * *

$\frac{9C}{5}=F-32$

**[1]**

> *Get **F** on its own (by adding 32 to both sides)  *

$\frac{9C}{5}+32=F$

$F=\frac{9C}{5}+32$* ***[1]**

*Method 2*

*Expand the brackets* * *

$9C=5F-160$ * *

*Get 5**F** on its own (by adding 160 to both sides)* * *

$9C+160=5F$

**[1]**

> *Get **F** on its own (by dividing both sides by 5)  *

$\frac{9C+160}{5}=F$

$F=\frac{9C+160}{5}$** [1]**

**either answers from Method 1 or Method 2 are accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $a$ the subject of the formula  $p=\frac{3a+5}{4-a}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove fractions (by multiplying both sides by (4 - **a**)* * *

$p \left(4 - a\right) = 3 a + 5$

**[1]**

*Expanding the brackets (by multiplying each term inside by **p**)* * *

$4p-pa=3a+5$ * *

*Get the **a** terms on one side (for example, by adding **pa** to both sides then subtracting 5 from both sides)* * *

$\begin{aligned}4 p & = & 3 a + 5 + a p \\ 4 p - 5 & = & 3 a + a p\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise **a** out of the terms on the right* * *

$4 p - 5 = a \left(3 + p\right)$

**[1]**

*Get **a** on its own (by dividing both sides by 3 + **p**)* * *

$\frac{4p-5}{3+p}=a$

$a=\frac{4p-5}{3+p}$* ***[1]**

$a=\frac{5-4p}{-3-p}$* ***is also accepted**

parts.problemMd:
$m=\sqrt{\frac{k+1}{4}}$

Make $k$ the subject of the formula.
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove the square-root sign (by squaring both sides)* * *

$m^{2}=\frac{k+1}{4}$

**[1]**

*Get **k** + 1 on its own (by multiplying both sides by 4)* * *

$4m^{2}=k+1$

**[1]**

*Get **k** on its own (by subtracting 1 from both sides)* * *

$4m^{2}-1=k$

$k=4m^{2}-1$** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Make $t$ the subject of the formula $p=at--d$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **t** first, the **at** term by adding **d** to both sides.*

$p+d=at$

**[1]**

> *Isolate **t** by dividing both sides by **a**.*

$\frac{p+d}{a}=t$

$\thereforet=\frac{p+d}{a}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$t=\frac{p}{a}+\frac{d}{a}$**.**

parts.problemMd:
Make $t$ the subject of the formula

$p=\frac{3-2t}{4+t}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove fractions (by multiplying both sides by 4 + **t**)* * *

$p \left(4 + t\right) = 3 - 2 t$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying each term inside by **p**)* * *

$4p+pt=3-2t$ * *

*Move the **t** terms to one side (for example, by adding 2**t** to both sides then subtracting 4**p** from both sides)* * *

$\begin{aligned}4 p + p t + 2 t & = & 3 \\ p t + 2 t & = & 3 - 4 p\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise **t** out of the terms on the left* * *

$t \left(p + 2\right) = 3 - 4 p$

**[1]**

> *Get **t** on its own (by dividing both sides by** p** + 2)*

$t=\frac{3-4p}{p+2}$* ***[1]**

$t=\frac{4p-3}{-p-2}$** is also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $m$the subject of   $g-3m=am+5$
parts.solutionMd:
*Get the **m** terms on to one side (for example, by adding 3**m** to both sides)* * *

$g=am+5+3m$ * *

*Get the **m** terms on their own (by subtracting 5 from both sides)* * *

$g-5=am+3m$

**[1]**

*am** and 3**m** are not "like" terms* *Factorise **m** out of these two terms* * *

$g - 5 = m \left(a + 3\right)$

**[1]**

*Get **m** on its own (by dividing both sides by **a** + 3)* * *

$\frac{g-5}{a+3}=m$

$m=\frac{g-5}{a+3}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Make $a$ the subject of $d=g+2ac$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **a** first, the 2**ac** term by subtracting **g** from both sides.*

$d-g=2ac$

**[1]**

> *Isolate **a** by dividing both sides by 2**c**.*

$\frac{d-g}{2c}=a$

$\thereforea=\frac{d-g}{2c}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$a=\frac{d}{2c}-\frac{g}{2c}$**.**

parts.problemMd:
Make $m$ the subject of

$\frac{m}{v}-\frac{t}{b}=\frac{m-t}{R}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Get rid of fractions (by multiplying both sides by **bvR**)* * *

$\begin{aligned}b v R \left(\frac{m}{v} - \frac{t}{b}\right) & = & b v R \times \frac{\left(m - t\right)}{R} \\ & & \\ \frac{b \cancel{v} R m}{\cancel{v}} - \frac{\cancel{b} v R t}{\cancel{b}} & = & \frac{b v \cancel{R} \left(m - t\right)}{\cancel{R}} \\ & & \\ b R m - v R t & = & b v \left(m - t\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets on the right* * *

$bRm-vRt=bvm-bvt$ * *

*Move all the **m** terms on to one side (for example, by subtracting **bvm** from both sides then adding **vRt** to both sides)* * *

$\begin{aligned}b R m - v R t - b v m & = & - b v t \\ b R m - b v m & = & v R t - b v t\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise **m** out of the terms on the left* * *

$m \left(b R - b v\right) = v R t - b v t$

**[1]**

> *Get **m** on its own (by dividing both sides by **bR - bv**)*

$m=\frac{vRt-bvt}{bR-bv}$* ***[1]**

$m=\frac{bvt-vRt}{bv-bR}$* ***is also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $c$ the subject of $A=\frac{c}{y}-5z$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **c** first, the *$\frac{c}{y}$* term by adding 5**z** to both sides.*

$A+5z=\frac{c}{y}$

**[1]**

> *Isolate **c** by multiplying both sides by **y**.*

$y \left(A + 5 z\right) = c$

$\thereforec=y(A+5z)$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$c=Ay+5yz$**.**

parts.problemMd: Make $a$ the subject of the formula $M=ac--bd$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **a** first, the **ac** term by adding **bd** to both sides.*

$M+bd=ac$

**[1]**

> *Isolate **a** by dividing both sides by **c**.*

$\frac{M+bd}{c}=a$

$\thereforea=\frac{M+bd}{c}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$a=\frac{M}{c}+\frac{bd}{c}$**.**

parts.problemMd: Make $m$ the subject of the formula  $f=\frac{3m+4}{m-1}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove fractions (by multiplying both sides by **m** - 1)* * *

$f \left(m - 1\right) = 3 m + 4$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying each term inside by **f**)* * *

$fm-f=3m+4$ * *

*Get all the **m** terms on one side (for example, by subtracting 3**m** from both sides then adding **f **to both sides)* * *

$\begin{aligned}f m - f - 3 m & = & 4 \\ f m - 3 m & = & 4 + f\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise **m** out of the terms on the left* * *

$m \left(f - 3\right) = 4 + f$

*Get **m** on its own (by dividing both sides by **f** - 3)* * *

$m=\frac{4+f}{f-3}$* ***[1]**

$m=\frac{-f-4}{3-f}$** is also accepted**

parts.problemMd: Make $f$ the subject of $m=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}ef}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **f**, the *$\frac{1}{3}ef$* term, by squaring both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}m^{2} & = & \frac{1}{3} e f\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 3.*

$3m^{2}=ef$

> *Isolate **f** by dividing both sides by **e**.*

$\frac{3m^{2}}{e}=f$

$\thereforef=\frac{3m^{2}}{e}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$f=3m^{2}e^{-1}$**.**

parts.problemMd: Make $e$ the subject of the formula $h=3e+f$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **e** first, the **3e** term by subtracting **f** from both sides.*

$h-f=3e$

**[1]**

> *Isolate **e** by dividing both sides by 3.*

$\frac{h-f}{3}=e$

$\thereforee=\frac{h-f}{3}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$e = \frac{1}{3} \left(h - f\right)$**.**

parts.problemMd: Make *t *the subject of  $n^{2}=\frac{4d+t^{3}}{t^{3}}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove fractions (by multiplying both sides by **t*<sup>*3*</sup>*)* * *

$t^{3}n^{2}=4d+t^{3}$

**[1]**

*Collect all the terms in **t** on one side (subtract **t*<sup>*3*</sup>* from both sides)* * *

$t^{3}n^{2}-t^{3}=4d$ * *

*'Factorise out' the the **t*<sup>*3*</sup> * *

$\begin{aligned}t^{3} \left(n^{2} - 1\right) & = & 4 d\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*And divide both sides by '**n*<sup>*2*</sup>* − 1' to leave **t*<sup>*3*</sup>* on its own on the left hand side* * *

$\begin{aligned}t^{3} & = & \frac{4 d}{n^{2} - 1}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Take the cube root of both sides* * *

$\mathbf{\mathit{t}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{4 \mathbf{\mathit{d}}}{\mathbf{\mathit{n}}^{2} - 1}}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Rearrange $y=\sqrt{w^{3}}$ to make $w$ the subject.

Circle your answer.

| $w=y^{6}$ | $w  = \sqrt[3]{y^{2}}$ | $w=\sqrt{y^{3}}$ | $w=y^{5}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *Square both sides of the equation.*

$y^{2}=w^{3}$

> *Take the cube root of both sides.*

$\sqrt[3]{y^{2}} = w$

$\mathbf{\mathit{w}} = \sqrt[3]{\mathbf{\mathit{y}}^{2}}$ **[1]**

> *If you square both sides and then multiply the powers together on the *$y$*, you will get the incorrect answer of *$w=y^{6}$*.*

> *If you copy the operations that are initially acting on the *$w$* (cube and square root) and copy them on to the *$y$* instead, you will get the incorrect answer of *$w=\sqrt{y^{3}}$*.*

> *If you square both sides and then add the powers together on the *$y$*, you will get the incorrect answer of *$w=y^{5}$*.*

parts.problemMd: Make $t$ the subject of        $c=t^{3}-8v$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **t** first, the **t*<sup>*3*</sup>* term by adding 8**v** to both sides.*

$c+8v=t^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Isolate **t** by taking the cube root of both sides.*

$\sqrt[3]{c + 8 v} = t$

$\therefore \mathbf{\mathit{t}} = \sqrt[3]{\mathbf{c} + 8 \mathbf{v}}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$t = \left(c + 8 v\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}$**.**

parts.problemMd: Make $c$ the subject of the formula  $p=\sqrt{\frac{ac+8}{3+c}}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by squaring both sides to remove the square root.*

$p^{2}=\frac{ac+8}{3+c}$

**[1]**

> *Remove fractions by multiplying (both sides) by 3 + **c.*

$p^{2} \left(3 + c\right) = a c + 8$

> *Expand the brackets by multiplying each term inside by p*<sup>*2*</sup>*. *

$3p^{2}+cp^{2}=ac+8$

**[1]**

*Being all the **c** terms to one side (for example, by subtracting **ac** from both sides then adding 3**p*<sup>*2*</sup>* **to both sides)* * *

$\begin{aligned}3 p^{2} + c p^{2} - a c & = & 8 \\ c p^{2} - a c & = & 8 - 3 p^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise **c** from the terms on the left-hand side.* * *

$c \left(p^{2} - a\right) = 8 - 3 p^{2}$

> *Isolate **c** by dividing (both sides) by **p*<sup>*2*</sup>* - a.*

$c=\frac{8-3p^{2}}{p^{2}-a}$

*There is nothing to simplify or rearrange so this is the final answer.* * *

$c=\frac{8-3p^{2}}{p^{2}-a}$* ***[1]**

**Equivalent expressions allowed such as **$c=\frac{3p^{2}-8}{a-p^{2}}$**.**

parts.problemMd: Rearrange  $a=\frac{b}{c}+5$  to make $c$ the subject.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by subtracting 5 from both sides to isolate the term involving **c**.*

$a-5=\frac{b}{c}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by c to remove the fraction.*

$c \left(a - 5\right) = b$

**[1]**

> *To make **c** the subject, divide both sides by (**a** - 5).*

$c=\frac{b}{a-5}$

$c=\frac{b}{a-5}$ **[1]**

**Ensure that " ****c**** = " is included in your final answer to gain full marks.**

parts.problemMd:
Rearrange$y=3x--2$ to make x the subject.

Circle your answer.

| $x=\frac{y}{3}-2$ | $x=\frac{y+2}{3}$ | $x=\frac{y-2}{3}$ | $x=\frac{y}{3}+2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *Add 2 to both sides of the equation.*

$y+2=3x$

> *Divide both sides by 3.*

$\frac{y+2}{3}=x$

$x=\frac{y+2}{3}$ **[1]**

> *If you divide the left hand side by 3, then subtract 2 from both sides, you get the incorrect answer of *$x=\frac{y}{3}-2$*.*

> *If you subtract 2 from both sides, then divide both sides by 3, you get the incorrect answer of *$x=\frac{y-2}{3}$*.*

> *If you divide the left hand side by 3, then add 2 to both sides you get the incorrect answer of *$x=\frac{y}{3}+2$*.*

parts.problemMd: Make $x$the subject of $y=\sqrt{\frac{x+1}{x-4}}$
parts.solutionMd:
*Remove the square root by squaring both sides.* * *

$y^{2}=\frac{x+1}{x-4}$

**[1]**

*Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by the denominator (**x** - 4).* * *

$y^{2} \left(x - 4\right) = x + 1$

**[1]*** *

> *Expand the brackets on the left hand side of the formula.*

$\begin{aligned}x y^{2} - 4 y^{2} & = & x + 1\end{aligned}$

> *Collect x terms on the same side of the formula - and everything else on the other side (by subtracting **x** from, and adding 4**y*<sup>*2*</sup>* to, both sides)*

$xy^{2}-x=4y^{2}+1$

**[1]**

*Factorise **x** out of the terms on the left hand side* * *

$x \left(y^{2} - 1\right) = 4 y^{2} + 1$

*Get **x** on its own (by dividing both sides by **y*<sup>*2*</sup>* - 1)* * *

$x=\frac{4y^{2}+1}{y^{2}-1}$

$x=\frac{4y^{2}+1}{y^{2}-1}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Use the formula $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$.

Make $a$ the subject of the formula.

$a$ = ..................
parts.solutionMd:
> *Isolate the term involving **a **by subtracting **ut** from both sides of the formula.*

$s-ut=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$

> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by its denominator, 2.*

$2 \left(s - u t\right) = a t^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Finally, to isolate **a**, divide both sides by **t*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\frac{2 \left(s - u t\right)}{t^{2}} = a$

$a=\frac{2(s-ut)}{t^{2}}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Rearrange $v=u+at$  to make $t$ the subject of the formula.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by subtracting **u** from both sides.*

$v-u=at$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by **a**.*

$\frac{v-u}{a}=t$

$\thereforet=\frac{v-u}{a}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Make $t$ the subject of $s=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> 'Make t the subject' means to rearrange the given formula so that it begins with  $t=$

> *Rearrange the formula, using the balance method and doing the same thing to both sides of the equation at each step*

> *The inverse of *$\frac{1}{2}$* is to multiply both sides by 2 giving:*

$\begin{aligned}s & = & \frac{1}{2} a t^{2} \\ 2 s & = & a t^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Divide both sides by *$a$

$\begin{aligned}\frac{2 s}{a} & = & t^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Square root both sides*

$\begin{aligned}\pm \sqrt{\frac{2 s}{a}} & = & t\end{aligned}$

$t=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Awarded for a correct first step in rearranging the formula. E.g. $2s=at^{2}$ or $\frac{s}{a}=\frac{1}{2}t^{2}$ or $\frac{2s}{a}=t^{2}$
> 
> **A1**: This mark is still awarded with $\pm$ omitted in final answer.

parts.problemMd: Given that $n>0$ make $n$ the subject of the formula $y=\frac{n^{2}+d}{n^{2}}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by the denominator (**n*<sup>*2*</sup>*).*

$yn^{2}=n^{2}+d$

**[1]*** *

> *Collect **n** terms on the same side of the formula (by subtracting **n*<sup>*2*</sup>* from both sides).*

$yn^{2}-n^{2}=d$

**[1]**

> *Factorise **n*<sup>*2*</sup>* out of the terms on the left hand side.*

$n^{2} \left(y - 1\right) = d$

**[1]**

> *Get **n*<sup>*2*</sup>* on its own (by dividing both sides by **y** - 1).*

$n^{2}=\frac{d}{y-1}$

> *Now square root, but we are given that *$n>0$* so we only need the positive square root.*

$n=\sqrt{\frac{d}{y-1}}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Rearrange this formula to make *y* the subject.

*x* = *y*<sup>2 </sup>+ 7
parts.solutionMd:
> *Subtract 7 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}x - 7 & = & y^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *It may be easier here to swap the left and right sides, although it is not necessary.*

$\begin{aligned}y^{2} & = & x - 7 \end{aligned}$

> *Take the square root of both sides, remember that a square root can be both positive or negative.*

$\begin{aligned} y^{2} & = & x - 7 \\ \sqrt{} & = & \sqrt{} \\ y & = & \pm \sqrt{x - 7}\end{aligned}$

$y=\pm\sqrt{x-7}$** [1]**

** ± sign not necessary for full marks**

parts.problemMd: Rearrange $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}}$ to make $x$ the subject.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First square both sides of the formula to remove the square root.*

$\begin{aligned}y^{2} & = & \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 1}}\right)^{2} \\ y^{2} & = & \frac{\left(1\right)^{2}}{\left(\sqrt{x + 1}\right)^{2}} \\ y^{2} & = & \frac{1}{x + 1}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by the denominator to remove the fraction.*

$y^{2} \left(x + 1\right) = 1$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets on the left-hand side.*

$xy^{2}+y^{2}=1$

> *Isolate the **x** term by subtracting **y*<sup>*2*</sup>* from both sides.*

$xy^{2}=1-y^{2}$

> *Finally divide both sides by **y*<sup>*2*</sup>* to make **x** the subject.*

$x=\frac{1-y^{2}}{y^{2}}$

$x=\frac{1-y^{2}}{y^{2}}$ **[1]**

> *Isolate the term involving **x** by adding 3 to both sides of the equation.*

$y+3=7x$

**[1]**

> *Isolate x by dividing boths sides by 7.*

$\frac{y+3}{7}=x$

$x=\frac{y+3}{7}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Make $e$ the subject of $w=\sqrt{\frac{e+g}{ef-d}}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Square both sides*

$\begin{aligned}w & = & \sqrt{\frac{e + g}{e f - d}} \\ w^{2} & = & \frac{e + g}{e f - d}\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Multiply by the denominator and expand the brackets*

$\begin{aligned}w^{2} \left(e f - d\right) & = & e + g \\ e f w^{2} - d w^{2} & = & e + g\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Rearrange to have all the terms containing *$e$* on one side*

$\begin{aligned}e f w^{2} - d w^{2} - e & = & g \\ e f w^{2} - e & = & g + d w^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Take out a factor of *$e$* on the left side*

$e \left(f w^{2} - 1\right) = g + d w^{2}$

> *Divide by the term in the brackets to leave *$e$* on the left*

$e=\frac{g+dw^{2}}{fw^{2}-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **A1**: If you rearrange to put all the $e$ terms on the right hand side earlier in your method, you may have one of the following equivalent versions of this answer:
> 
> $e=\frac{-g-dw^{2}}{1-fw^{2}}\mathrm{or}e=-\frac{g+dw^{2}}{1-fw^{2}}$
> 
> One of these will also get the marks.

parts.problemMd: Make $n$ the subject of the formula $x=\frac{3p+n}{3n-4}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Remove the fraction by multiplying both sides by the denominator*

$x \left(3 n - 4\right) = 3 p + n$

> *Expand the brackets*

$3nx-4x=3p+n$

**[M1]**

> *Collect the *$n$* terms on one side by subtracting *$n$* from both sides*

$3nx-n-4x=3p$

> *Move any other terms to the other side by using the inverse operation*

> *Add *$4x$* to both sides*

$3nx-n=3p+4x$

**[M1]**

> *Take out a factor of *$n$

$n \left(3 x - 1\right) = 3 p + 4 x$

> *Divide by the bracket to leave *$n$* as the subject*

$n=\frac{3p+4x}{3x-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> You must have "$n=$" as part of your final answer.

parts.problemMd:
An arithmetic series has first term $a$ and common difference $d$. 

The sum of the first $2n$ terms of the series is four times the sum of the first $n$ terms of the series.

Find an expression for a in terms of $d$. 
Show your working clearly.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for 2**n.*

> $S_{2 n} = \frac{2 n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right] = n \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right]$* *

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for **n.*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$* *

> *S*<sub>*2n *</sub>*= 4 × **S*<sub>*n*</sub>* , use this to form an equation in terms of **a, d **and **n**.*

> $n \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right] = 4 \left(\frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify and cancel **n **from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(a + 5 d\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(a + 5 d\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the second equation by substituting *$a=6-3d$* in. *

$\begin{aligned}\left(\left(6 - 3 d\right) + 5 d\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(\left(6 - 3 d\right) + 5 d\right) \\ \left(6 + 2 d\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(6 + 2 d\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets and rearrange to form a quadratic equation in terms of **d.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(6 + 2 d\right) \left(6 + 2 d\right) + 18 & = & 66 + 22 d \\ 36 + 12 d + 12 d + 4 d^{2} + 18 & = & 66 + 22 d \\ 4 d^{2 } + 24 d + 54 & = & 66 + 22 d \\ 4 d^{2 } + 2 d - 12 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]*** *

> *Simplify**.*

$\begin{aligned}2 d^{2 } + d - 6 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

> *Be sure to **show** the stages of using the quadratic formula - only use your calculator to check your answers.*

$a=2,b=1,c=-6$

parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for the first 48 terms of an arithmetic series (**n** = 48).*

> $S_{48} = \frac{48}{2} \left[2 a + \left(48 - 1\right) d\right] = 24 \left(2 a + 47 d\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for the first 36 terms of the same arithmetic series (**n** = 36).*

> $S_{36} = \frac{36}{2} \left[2 a + \left(36 - 1\right) d\right] = 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)$* *

> *S*<sub>*48 *</sub>*= 4 × **S*<sub>*36*</sub>* , use this to form an equation in terms of **a **and **d**.*

> $24 \left(2 a + 47 d\right) = 4 \left( 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify by canceling 4 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned} \frac{24 \left(2 a + 47 d\right)}{4} & = & \frac{4 \left( 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\right)}{4} \\ 6 \left(2 a + 47 d\right) & = & 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify by canceling 6 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{ 6 \left(2 a + 47 d\right)}{6} & = & \frac{18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)}{6} \\ 2 a + 47 d & = & 3 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets on the right-hand side.*

> $\begin{aligned}2 a + 47 d & = & 6 a + 105 d\end{aligned}$* *

> *Rearrange to make **a** (or **d**) the subject.*

$\begin{aligned}2 a - 6 a & = & 105 d - 47 d \\ - 4 a & = & 58 d \\ a & = & \frac{58 d}{- 4} = - 14 . 5 d\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for the first 30 terms of an arithmetic series (**n** = 30).*

> $S_{30} = \frac{30}{2} \left[2 a + \left(30 - 1\right) d\right] = 15 \left(2 a + 29 d\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Substitute **a **= -14.5**d **into the expression found for **S*<sub>*30.*</sub>* *

> $S_{30} = 15 \left(2 \left(- 14 . 5 d\right) + 29 d\right) = 15 \left(- 29 d + 29 d\right) = 15 \times 0$* *

$S_{30}=0$ **[1]**

> *In the first year, Mario saves \$50, so **a **= 50. *

> *Each year Mario increases the amount saved by \$**k** so** d** = **k**.*

**[1]**

> *The total amount Mario will save is \$33 125, so **S*<sub>*n*</sub>* = 33 125. Substitute these values into the formula for the sum of an arithmetic sequence.*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} [ 2 a + ( n - 1 ) d ]$

> *Divide by 49 to find the value of **k.** *

$\begin{aligned}k & = & \frac{1225}{49}\end{aligned}$

$k=25$ **[1]**

The sum of the first 10 terms of $A$ is 290

Find the 10th term of $A$.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula for an arithmetic sequence is $u_{n} = a + \left(n - 1\right) d$ where $a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference.

> *Form an equation using the fact that the third term is 19*

$a+2d=19$

**[M1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula for the sum of the first  $n$ terms of an arithmetic sequence is $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$ where $a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference.

> *Form an equation using the fact that the sum of the first 10 terms is 290*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{10}{2} \left(2 a + \left(10 - 1\right) d\right) & = & 290 \\ 5 \left(2 a + 9 d\right) & = & 290 \\ 10 a + 45 d & = & 290\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Now that two equations have been formed in terms of *$a$* and *$d$*, they can be solved simultaneously using the elimination method for example*

> **[exam-tip]**
> The elimination method or substitution method for solving simultaneous equations will give the same solutions.
> 
> Once you have solved for both variables always substitute both values into one equation to check they work together, although this working is not required to gain full marks.

> *The simultaneous equations to solve are:*

$\begin{aligned}10 a + 45 d & = & 290 \\ a + 2 d & = & 19\end{aligned}$

> *First equate coefficients of one variable by multiplying one or both of the equations*

> *In this case multiply the second equation by 10 to equate the coefficients of *$a$

$\begin{aligned}10 a + 45 d & = & 290 \\ 10 a + 20 d & = & 190\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract the second equation from the first equation to eliminate *$a$* and then solve for *$d$

$\begin{aligned}10 a + 45 d & = & 290 - \\ 10 a + 20 d & = & 190\end{aligned}$

*----------------*

$\begin{aligned}25 d & = & 100 \\ d & = & \frac{100}{25} \\ d & = & 4\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Substitute the value of *$d$* into one of the original equations (either will work) and solve for *$a$

> *Substituting into *$a+2d=19$* gives:*

$\begin{aligned}a + 2 \left(4\right) & = & 19 \\ a + 8 & = & 19 \\ a & = & 19 - 8 \\ a & = & 11\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute both values into the other equation to check both solutions work together*

> *Substituting into *$10a+45d=290$* gives:*

$\begin{aligned}10 \left(11\right) + 45 \left(4\right) & = & 290 \\ 110 + 180 & = & 290\end{aligned}$

*The solutions satisfy the equation*

> *Substitute these values into the formula for  *$u_{n}$*to find the 10th term*

$11 + \left(10 - 1\right) \times 4$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **47**

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
The sum of the first 80 terms of an arithmetic series, *S*, is 470

The 75th term of *S* is 14.5

The sum of the first *X* terms of S is 171

Work out the value of *X* 
Show your working clearly
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> This question is giving you information in steps so that you can form simultaneous equations.

> *Use the formula for the sum of a series for the sum of 80 terms to create an equation*

$\begin{aligned}S_{n} & = & \frac{ n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right] \\ S_{80} & = & 470 \\ 470 & = & \frac{ 80}{2} \left(2 a + 79 d\right)\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Then use the information about the 75th term to create another equation so that you have simultaneous equations*

$a+74d=14.5$

**[M1]**

> *Solve your equations simultaneously*

$\begin{aligned}470 & = & \frac{80}{2} \left(2 a + 79 d\right) \\ 14 . 5 & = & a + 74 d\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify the first equation and divide it by 40 *

> *Multiply the second equation by 2 to get the same coefficient of a*

$\begin{aligned}11 . 75 & = & 2 a + 79 d \\ 29 & = & 2 a + 148 d\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Subtract the first equation from the second equation and solve to find d*

$\begin{aligned}17 . 25 & = & 69 d \\ d & = & 0 . 25\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute d= 0.25 back into one of the original equations and solve to find a*

$\begin{aligned}a + 74 \left(0 . 25\right) & = & 14 . 5 \\ a + 18 . 5 & = & 14 . 5 \\ a & = & - 4\end{aligned}$

**[A1]**

> *Use the sum of the series formula with your values of a and d and the total 171 to create an equation with X*

$\begin{aligned}S_{X} & = & \frac{X}{2} \left[2 \left(- 4\right) + 0 . 25 \left(X - 1\right)\right] \\ 171 & = & \frac{ X}{2} \left(- 8 + 0 . 25 X - 0 . 25\right)\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Solve the equation to find X*

$\begin{aligned}342 & = & X \left(0 . 25 X - 8 . 25\right) \\ 0 & = & 0 . 25 X^{2} - 8 . 25 X - 342\end{aligned}$

> *Use the quadratic formula to solve this*

$X = \frac{8.25 \pm \sqrt{ ( - 8.25 ) ^{2} - 4 \times 0.25 \times ( - 342 ) }}{2}$
X space equals space 57 space o r space minus 24

> *The term number cannot be negative*

$X=57$

**[A1]**

144 space plus space 36 N space equals space 60 space N
