parts.problemMd:
The total surface area of a solid hemisphere is equal to the curved surface area of a cylinder.

The radius of the hemisphere is $r$ cm. 
The radius of the cylinder is twice the radius of the hemisphere.

Given that

$\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{hemisphere}:\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{cylinder}=1:m$

find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The total surface area of a hemisphere is*

$\begin{aligned}S A_{h e m i s p h e r e} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \pi r^{2} + \pi r^{2} \\ & = & 3 \pi r^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Now that we have used *$r$* as the radius of the hemisphere, let *$R$* be the radius of the cylinder (and let its height be *$h$*). The curved surface area of the cylinder is therefore*

$SA_{cylinder}=2πRh$

> *"The radius of the cylinder is twice the radius of the hemisphere" therefore*

$R=2r$

> *Substitute this into the formula for the curved surface area of the cylinder*

$\begin{aligned}S A_{c y l i n d e r} & = & 2 \pi \left(2 r\right) h \\ & = & 4 \pi r h\end{aligned}$

> *Equate the formulae for the surface areas of the hemisphere and the cylinder*

$3πr^{2}=4πrh$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to get *$h$* in terms of *$r$

$\begin{aligned}3 \cancel{\pi} r^{2} & = & 4 \cancel{\pi} r h \\ 3 r^{\cancel{2}} & = & 4 \cancel{r} h \\ 3 r & = & 4 h \\ h & = & \frac{3}{4} r\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the volume of the hemisphere in terms of *$r$

$\begin{aligned}v o l u m e_{h e m i s p h e r e} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} \\ & = & \frac{2}{3} \pi r^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *And find the volume of the cylinder in terms of *$r$

$\begin{aligned}v o l u m e_{c y l i n d e r} & = & \pi R^{2} h \\ & = & \pi \left(2 r\right)^{2} \times \frac{3}{4} r \\ & = & \pi \cancel{4} r^{2} \times \frac{3}{\cancel{4}} r \\ & = & 3 \pi r^{3}\end{aligned}$

** correct expressions for volume of hemisphere and volume of cylinder ****[1]**

> $m$*, the scale factor for the volumes, is the volume of the cylinder divided by the volume of the hemisphere*

$\begin{aligned}m & = & \frac{3 \pi r^{3}}{\frac{2}{3} \pi r^{3}} = \frac{3 \cancel{\pi r^{3}}}{\frac{2}{3} \cancel{\pi r^{3}}} \\ & = & 3 \times \frac{3}{2} \\ & = & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$

$m=\frac{9}{2}\mathrm{or}4.5$ **[1]**

$k=\sqrt{\frac{25}{9}}=\frac{5}{3}$

$\frac{5}{3}$** ****or**** **$\frac{3}{5}$**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}k^{3} & = & \left(\sqrt{\frac{25}{9}}\right)^{3} = \left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^{3} = \frac{125}{27}\end{aligned}$

> *(Note that the two steps above can be performed in one step: *$k^{3} = \left(\sqrt{\frac{25}{9}}\right)^{3}$

$135\times\frac{125}{27}$

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> *If the ratio for the areas of similar shapes is *$m^{2}:n^{2}$*, then the linear ratio (ratio for corresponding lengths) for those shapes is *$m:n$* and the ratio for the volumes of the similar shapes is *$m^{3}:n^{3}$*.*

> *First find the linear ratio by square rooting the area ratio.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}linear scale factor & = & \sqrt{16} : \sqrt{25} \\ & = & 4 : 5\end{aligned}$

> *Next find the volume ratio by cubing the linear ratio.*

$\begin{aligned}volume scale factor & = & 4^{3} : 5^{3} \\ & = & 64 : 125\end{aligned}$

**The third option is correct, 64 : 125*** ***[1]**

> *The first option, "4 : 5", is the length ratio.*

> *The second option, "16 : 25", is the area (or surface area) ratio.*

> *The fourth option, "256 : 625", is the linear ratio to the power of 4; "4*<sup>*4*</sup>* : 5*<sup>*4*</sup>*". This is not useful for Area & Volume of Similar Shapes questions.*

parts.problemMd:
Solids $X$ and $Y$ are similar.

$X$ has volume 64 cm<sup>3</sup> 
$Y$ has volume 343 cm<sup>3</sup>

The surface area of $X$ is 176 cm<sup>2</sup> 
Work out the surface area of $Y$.

..........................cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of Solid X and Solid Y are in the ratio 64 : 343. And if the volumes of two solids are in the ratio *$m^{3}:n^{3}$*, then the corresponding lengths are in the ratio *$m:n$* and corresponding areas are in the ratio *$m^{2}:n^{2}$*.*

> *First find the linear ratio (ratio of corresponding lengths) in X and Y by cube rooting the volume ratio.*

$\sqrt[3]{64} : \sqrt[3]{343} = 4 : 7$

**[1]**

> *Now find the area (or surface area) ratio by squaring the linear ratio.*

$4^{2}:7^{2}=16:49$

**[1]**

> *Now use the area ratio with the surface area of X to find the surface area of Y, which we will call *$y$*.*

$16:49=176:y$

> *We can find **y** by scaling up the ratio. 176 ÷ 16 = 11 so both sides of the ratio need to be multiplied by 11.*

$16:49\,\times11\times11\,=176:49\times11\,=176:539$

**The surface area of Y = 539 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1]**

> *Alternatively, from *$16:49=176:y$*, we could convert to a fraction and solve:*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{176}{16} & = & \frac{y}{49} \\ y & = & 49 \times \frac{176}{16} \\ & = & 539\end{aligned}$

![q5-paper6-nov2018-ocr-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/bearings-scale-drawing-and-constructions/assets/072-q5-paper6-nov2018-ocr-gcse-maths.png)

Neil knows that Packer Street is 180m long in real life.

i) Neil measures the map. 
He says

Packer Street is 3.5cm long.
    High Street is 11.2cm long.
    Therefore, I calculate that High Street is 576m long in real life.

Use Neil’s figures to show that the answer to his calculation is correct.

[3]

ii) Jodie measures the same map.

She says

I think Packer Street is longer than Neil’s measurement of 3.5cm.
    Therefore, High Street must be longer than 576m in real life.

Is Jodie’s reasoning correct? 
Show how you decide.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *Use the map and real life measurements for Packer Street to write the scale for the map.*

*3.5 cm represents 180 m*

> *Divide the real life measurement by the map measurement to find how many real life metres is represented by a centimetre on the map.*

*180 ÷ 3.5 = 51.4285...* *1 cm represents 51.4285... m*

**[1]**

> *Multiply by the map measurement for High Street. Use the answer button or type the calculation in as a single calculation.*

*180 ÷ 3.5 × 11.2*

**[1]**

*= 576*

**The real life measurement for High Street is 576 m*** ***[1]**

ii)  *If the map measurement is higher than 3.5 cm then each cm on the map will represent fewer metres as 180 will be divided by a bigger number.*

**Jodie's reasoning is ****incorrect**** as 1 cm will represent a**** smaller distance in real life**** therefore High Street will be ****shorter than 576 m** 
**Correct explanation**** [1]** 
**Stating that the reasoning is incorrect**** [1] **
**It is acceptable to choose a measurement bigger than 3.5 cm and showing that the real life length is less than 576 m**

parts.problemMd:
On another map, Packer Street is 2.4cm long.

Express the scale of this map in the form 1 : $n$.

1 : ..................
parts.solutionMd:
> *The distance on the map is 2.4 cm and the distance in real life is 180 m. Convert the 180 m into cm by multiplying by 100.*

$180m=180\times100\mathrm{cm}=18000\mathrm{cm}$

> *Now the units are the same you can write as a ratio without the units.*

$2.4:180000$

> *To make the first part of the ratio 1, you need to divide both sides by 2.4.*

$1:\frac{18000}{2.4}$

**[1]**

$1:7500$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A model railway is built using the scale 1 : 87.

On the model railway, the distance between the rails is 16.5 mm.

![q13-paper6-nov2017-ocr-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/bearings-scale-drawing-and-constructions/assets/073-q13-paper6-nov2017-ocr-gcse-maths.png)

Calculate, in metres, the distance between the rails for a full-size train.

.................... metres
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the distance for a full-size train by multiplying by 87. This will give the distance in millimetres.*

$16.5\mathrm{mm}\times87=1435.5\mathrm{mm}$

**[1]**

> *Convert to metres. 1 cm = 10 mm and 1 m = 100 cm so divide by 10 and then by 100.*

$1435.5\div10\div100=1.4355$

**1.4355 metres** **[1] **
**It is acceptable to round to 1.436 or 1.44**

parts.problemMd:
The scale of a map is 1 cm represents 25 m.

i) The length of a path is 240 m.

Work out the length, in centimetres, of the path on the map.

...................................................... cm [1]

ii) The scale 1 cm represents 25 m can be written in the form 1: *k*.

Find the value of *k*.

*k* = ..................................................... [1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *1 cm represents 25 m. To find out how many centimetres represent 240 m, you need to see how many times 25 goes into 240.*

*240 ÷ 25 = 9.6*

**9.6 cm** **[1]**

ii) *To find the ratio you need to write both in the same units. 1 m = 100 cm so convert 25 m into cm by multiplying by 100.*

*25 × 100 = 2500*

> *Now they are in the same units you can write as a ratio.*

*1: 2500*

**k**** = 2500 ****[1]**

![q16-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/bearings-scale-drawing-and-constructions/assets/014-q16-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

Ship $B$ is due north of ship $A$. 
The bearing of ship $C$from ship $A$ is 120°

Calculate the bearing of ship $C$ from ship $B$. 
Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To find the bearing of **C** from **B**, you first need to work out the angle **ABC**. *
*However you currently do not have enough information to work that out.*

![bearings-hq2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/bearings-scale-drawing-and-constructions/assets/015-bearings-hq2.png)

> *You know the lengths of two sides and the angle between them. Therefore you can use the cosine rule to find the length of the third side.*

> *The formula for the cosine rule is *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$*, where **b** and **c** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **A** and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**. *
*Substitute **a** = **z**, **b** = 275, **c** = 150 and **A** = 120 into the formula.*

$z^{2} = 275^{2} + 150^{2} - 2 \left(275\right) \left(150\right) cos \left(120\right)$

**[1]**

> *Type the expression into your calculator altogether as one line. If you do it separately you need to remember the order of operations (multiplication before addition). Take the positive square root and leave as an exact answer or store in your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}z^{2} & = & 139375 \\ z & = & \sqrt{139375} \\ & = & 373 . 329613 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *You can now find the angle at **B** by using either the sine rule or the cosine rule.*

> *Method 1 - Using the sine rule*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **A** = **y**, **B** = 120, **a** = 275 and **b** = √139375 into the formula.*

$\frac{sin y}{275} = \frac{sin \left(120\right)}{\sqrt{139375}}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 275 and then use the inverse sin function on your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{sin \left(120\right)}{\sqrt{139375}} \times 275\right) \\ & = & 39 . 637403 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the bearing by subtracting from 180.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 180 - 39 . 637403 . . . \\ & = & 140 . 362596 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to the nearest degree.140*

$140^{\circ}(\mathrm{nearest} \mathrm{degree})$** [1]**

> *Method 2 - Using the cosine rule*

> *The formula for the cosine rule is *$\mathrm{cos}A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that form the angle **A **and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**. Substitute **A** = **y**, **a** = 275, **b** = 150 and **c** = √139375 into the formula.*

$cos y = \frac{150^{2} + \left(\sqrt{139375}\right)^{2} - 275^{2}}{2 \times 150 \times \sqrt{139375}}$

**[1]**

> *Use the inverse cos function on your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & cos^{- 1} \left(\frac{150^{2} + \left(\sqrt{139375}\right)^{2} - 275^{2}}{2 \times 150 \times \sqrt{139375}}\right) \\ & = & 39 . 637403 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the bearing by subtracting from 180.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 180 - 39 . 637403 . . . \\ & = & 140 . 362596 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to the nearest degree.140*

$140^{\circ}(\mathrm{nearest} \mathrm{degree})$** [1]**

$105+180=285$

$285-230=55$

**[1]**

> *To find the distance between **A **and **C **you need to know the angle opposite it in the triangle. You know an angle and the length of the side opposite to it, you also know another length so you can therefore find the angle opposite it by using the sine rule.*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **a** = 95, **b** = 180, **A** = **y** and **B** = 55 into the formula.*

$\frac{sin \left(y\right)}{95} = \frac{sin \left(55\right)}{180}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 95 and then find the angle by using the inverse sin function.*

$\begin{aligned}sin \left(y\right) & = & \frac{sin \left(55\right)}{180} \times 95 \\ y & = & sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{sin \left(55\right)}{180} \times 95\right) \\ y & = & 25 . 615534 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The interior angles of the triangle should add up to 180°. Use the answer button on your calculator to find the third angle.*

$\begin{aligned}Angle A C B & = & 180 - 55 - 25 . 615534 . . . \\ & = & 99 . 384465 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *You now have enough information to find the side **LN** using either the sine rule or the cosine rule.*

> *Method 1 - Using the sine rule*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{a}{\mathrm{sin}A}=\frac{b}{\mathrm{sin}B}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **a** = **x**, **b** = 180, **A** = 99.384465... (using the answer button) and **B** = 55 into the formula.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{sin \left(99 . 384465 . . .\right)} & = & \frac{180}{sin \left(55\right)} \\ x & = & \frac{180}{sin \left(55\right)} \times sin \left(99 . 384465 . . .\right) \\ x & = & 216 . 798523 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

$217\mathrm{km}(3\mathrm{sf})$** [1]**

> *Method 2 - Using the cosine rule*

> *The formula for the cosine rule is *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$*, where **b** and **c** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **A** and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**. Substitute **a** = **x**, **b** = 95, **c** = 180 and **A** = 99.384465... (using the answer button) into the formula.*

$x ^{2} = 95 ^{2} + 180 ^{2} - 2 ( 95 ) ( 180 ) cos ( 99.384465... )$
$x = \sqrt{95 ^{2} + 180 ^{2} - 2 ( 95 ) ( 180 ) \text{cos} ( 99.384465... ) }$
x equals 216.798523...

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures. *

$217\mathrm{km}(3\mathrm{sf})$** [1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *To prove that **ST  **is equal to** UT ** you will need to **prove **that the triangle **STU **is **isosceles**. This can be done by finding the angles. *

> *PQRST **is a regular pentagon, so the angle **TSU** is the exterior angle of a regular pentagon. *
*Exterior angles in any polygon add up to 360°. *
*A regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles.*

> * *`T S with hat on top U space equals 360 over 5 equals space 72 degree`

**[1]**

> *To find the size of angle **SUT**, you will need to consider circle theorems.*

> *Begin by joining the point **O** to the points **T** and **R,** marking all the radiuses of the circle as equal lengths on the diagram.*

> *TP** and **TR **are also tangents to the circle, so by the circle theorem 'A tangent always meets a radius at 90°', angles **ORQ **and **OTP **are both 90°. *

`O R with hat on top Q space equals space O T with hat on top P space equals 90 degree`* **(angle between tangent and radius)*

**[1]**

> *Mark these onto the diagram.*

![QLY1pOQ2_4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/051-qly1poq2-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2.png)

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2). A regular pentagon has 5 equal interior angles, therefore these can be found using the formula *$\frac{180 \left(5 - 2\right)}{5}$*.*

> * *$T \hat{P} Q = P \hat{Q} R = \frac{3 \left(180\right)}{5} = 108 \circ$

> *Add these angles to the diagram.*

![4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/052-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3.png)

> *PQROT  **is a pentagon, so the angle **ROT**  can be found by subtracting the other four angles from the sun of the angles in a pentagon.*

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2).*

$R \hat{O} T + O \hat{T} P + T \hat{P} Q + P \hat{Q} R + Q \hat{R} O = 180 \left(5 - 2\right) \circ = 540 \circ$

> *Substitute in the angles you know to find angle **ROT**.*

$\begin{aligned}R \hat{O} T + 90 \circ + 90 \circ + 108 \circ + 108 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T + 396 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T & = & 144 \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *By the circle theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, angle **ROT **is twice angle **RUT.*

$R \hat{O} T = 2 \left(R \hat{U} T\right) = 2 \left(S \hat{U} T\right)$

$S \hat{U} T = \frac{R \hat{O} T}{2} = \frac{144}{2} = 72 \circ$

**[1]**

> *This proves that angle **TSU **is equal to angle **SUT **and so triangle **STU **is isosceles.*

**Therefore ****ST ****= ****UT **
**All reasons given clearly [1]**

> *Using the properties of Intersecting Chords (internal intersection), we know that*

> *Now you can use the result *$5x=3y$* to turn that into a quadratic equation in only one variable.*

$\begin{aligned}5 x & = & 3 y so y = \frac{5}{3} x\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd:
$A,B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$.

![q20-4ma1-2hr-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/034-q20-4ma1-2hr-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

Angle $ABC=75^{\circ}$

The area of the shaded segment is 200cm<sup>2</sup>

Calculate the radius of the circle. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

...................................................... cm
parts.solutionMd:
> *Angle **AOC **is made by drawing lines from the points **A** and **C **on the circle which meet at the centre (**O**).*

*The circle theorem states that the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference.* 
*Therefore angle **AOC **is double angle **ABC**.*

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q5-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/035-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q5-diagram-1.png)

$\mathrm{Angle}AOC=2\times75^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of the sector **AOC **using the formula for area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$* and substituting the values into the formula, letting *$θ=150$* and *$r=r$*.*

$\mathrm{Area}_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{150}{360}\timesπ\timesr^{2}=\frac{5}{12}πr^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of the triangle **AOC **using the formula for area of a triangle *$=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}θ$* and substituting the values into the formula, letting *$θ=150$* and *$r=r$*.*

$\mathrm{Area}_{\mathrm{triangle}}=\frac{1}{2}\timesr\timesr\times\mathrm{sin}150=\frac{1}{4}r^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of the shaded region by subtracting the area of the triangle from the area of sector **AOC.*

$\mathrm{Area}_{\mathrm{shaded}}=\frac{5}{12}πr^{2}-\frac{1}{4}r^{2}$

> *Form an equation by setting the expression for the area of the shaded region equal to 200 cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\frac{5}{12}πr^{2}-\frac{1}{4}r^{2}=200$

**[1]**

> *Factorise out **r*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$r^{2} \left(\frac{5}{12} \pi - \frac{1}{4}\right) = 200$

> *Isolate **r*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$r^{2} = \frac{200}{\left(\frac{5}{12} \pi - \frac{1}{4}\right) }$

> *Solve to find **r **by taking the square root of both sides.*

$r = \sqrt{\frac{200}{\left(\frac{5}{12} \pi - \frac{1}{4}\right) }} = 13 . 74256 . . .$

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**radius = 13.7 cm**<sup>** **</sup>**(3 s.f.)**** [1] **
**Answers in the range 13.7 to 13.8 accepted**

parts.problemMd:
$A,B$ and $C$ are three points on the circumference of a circle, centre $O$.

$BD$ and $CD$ are tangents to the circle. 
$ABDC$ is a kite. 
Angle $BDC$ is $x$

![q29-paper-3h-nov-2021-aqa-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/015-q29-paper-3h-nov-2021-aqa-gcse-maths.png)

Prove that angle $ABO$is  $45^{\circ}--\frac{x}{4}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The line segments **OB **and **OC **are radii because they join the centre to the circumference.*

> * Angles **OBD** and **OCD **are where tangents meet a radius.*

*Angle ***OBD ***= angle*** OCD*** = 90°   (Angle between a tangent and a radius = 90°)*

> *ABDC **is a kite, so its angles add up to 360°. Find angle **BOC **in terms of *$x$*.*

** ***Angle ***BOC*** + angle ***BDC ***+ angle ***OBD*** + angle ***OCD *** = 360° *** ***Angle ***BOC*** + *$x$* + 90° + 90°*** *** = 360° *
*Angle ***BOC*** = 180 - *$x$*°*

**[1]**

> *Write down an expression for angle **BAC **in terms of *$x$*.*

*Angle ***BOC *** = 2 x angle ***BAC***   (Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference) Therefore angle ***BAC *** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*(Angle ***BOC***)*

*Angle ***BAC ***= *$\frac{1}{2} \left(180 - x\right) \circ = 90 - \frac{x}{2} \circ$

**[1]**

> *Adding the information to the diagram as you go will help to see the next step.*

![gcse-aqa-tq-circle-theorems-h-8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/016-gcse-aqa-tq-circle-theorems-h-8.png)

> *Kites are symmetrical, so the line **AD **is a line of symmetry. Add this line the the diagram and consider one of the triangles. The line of symmetry cuts both angle **BAC **and angle **BDC **in half. Find the angles **BAD **and **BDA**.*

*Angle ***BAD*** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*angle ***BAC*** = *$\frac{1}{2} \left(90 - \frac{x}{2}\right) = 45 - \frac{x}{4}$

*Angle ***BDA*** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*angle ***BDC*** = *$\frac{1}{2}x$

> *Looking at triangle **ABD **only. *

![gcse-aqa-tq-circle-theorems-h-8-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/017-gcse-aqa-tq-circle-theorems-h-8-diagram-2.png)

> *Angles in a triangle add up to 180°. Find angle **ABO **in terms of *$x$*by subtracting all the other angles in triangle **ABD **from 180°.*

** ***Angle ***ABO*** + angle ***OBD ***+ angle ***BDO*** + angle ***BAO *** = 180° (angles in a triangle add up to 180°) *** **
*Angle ***ABO*** + 90° + *$\frac{x}{2}$* + *$\left(45 - \frac{x}{4}\right)$* = 180° *
*Angle ***ABO*** = 180 - 90 - *$\left(45 - \frac{x}{4}\right)$* - *$\frac{x}{2}$

> *Simplify.*

**Angle ****ABO****  = **$45+\frac{x}{4}-\frac{x}{2}=45-\frac{x}{4}^{\circ}$**  ****[1] **
**Completely correct method leading to given answer with all reasons stated**** [1]**

Prove that $AC=BC$

> *The word 'bisect' means 'to cut in half', so angle **ABC **= angle **CBQ .*

*Angle*** ABC ***= angle ***CBQ*** = *$x^{\circ}$* (***CB ***bisects angle ***ABQ***).*

**[1]**

> *The alternate segment theorem states that an angle inside a triangle with all three vertices on the circumference of a circle is equal to the angle between the opposite side and a tangent.*

> *The angle *$x$* is between a tangent and a side of a triangle which has all three vertices on the circumference. So it is equal to the angle in the triangle opposite that side.*

*Angle*** BAC ***= *$x^{\circ}$* (alternate segment theorem).*

**[1]**

> *If angles **ABC **and **BAC **are equal, then and triangle **ABC **is isosceles with sides **AC **= **BC.*

*Base angles in an isosceles triangle are equal.*

**Angle ****ABC**** = angle ****BAC ****= **$x^{\circ}$** so triangle ****ABC ****is isosceles**** ****[1]**

Prove that $ABCD$  is **not **a cyclic quadrilateral.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°. *

> *To prove that **ABCD **is not a cyclic quadrilateral, we will need to show that the angles opposite each other do **not **add up to 180° for a single value of *$x$*.*

> *Form an equation using angles **BAD **and **CBD, **assuming that they do add up to 180°.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x + 92 & = & 180\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation to find the value of *$x$* for which these opposite angles do add up to 180°.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x & = & 180 - 92 \\ 4 x & = & 88 \\ x & = & \frac{88}{4} \\ x & = & 22 \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute this value of *$x$* into the angles **ABC **and **ADC.*

$\begin{aligned}Angle A B C & = & 5 \left(22\right) + 30 = 140 \circ\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}Angle A D C & = & \left(22\right) + 36 = 58 \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Show that for this value of *$x$*, the sum of the angles **ABC **and **ADC **is not 180°.*

$\begin{aligned}Angle A B C + Angle A D C & = & 140 \circ + 58 \circ \neq 180 \circ\end{aligned}$

**Opposite angles do not add to 180°** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$C,D$ and $E$ are points on a circle.

$CE=DE$ 
The tangent at $D$ is shown.

![q25-paper-2h-nov-2019-aqa-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/026-q25-paper-2h-nov-2019-aqa-gcse-maths.png)

Prove that   $y=3x$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The alternate segment theorem states that an angle inside a triangle with all three vertices on the circumference of a circle is equal to the angle between the opposite side and a tangent.*

> *The angle *$4x$* is between a tangent and a side of a triangle which has all three vertices on the circumference. So it is equal to the angle in the triangle opposite that side.*

*Angle ***CED ***= *$4x^{\circ}$** ***(alternate segment theorem)*

**[1]**

> *Angles in a triangle sum to 180° and triangle **CED  **is isosceles, so angle **ECD  **= angle **EDC.*

*Angle ***DCE  ***=** *$\frac{180-4x}{2}$* *
*(Base angles in an isosceles triangle are equal and angles in a triangle = 180°)*

**[1]**

> *Vertically opposite angles are equal, so angle **ACB  **= angle **DCE.*

*Angle ***ACB*** = angle ***DCE  ***=** *$\frac{180-4x}{2}$* *
*(Vertically opposite angles are equal)*

> *Angles in a triangle sum to 180°, so angle **ACB  **+ angle **ABC **+ angle** BAC **= 180°.*

* *$\frac{180-4x}{2}+90-x+y=180$* *
*(Angles in a triangle = 180°)*

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

> * *$\begin{aligned} 90 - 2 x + 90 - x + y & = & 180 \\ 90 + 90 - 2 x - x + y & = & 180 \\ 180 - 3 x + y & = & 180\end{aligned}$

> *Cancel 180 from both sides and rearrange to make **y **the subject.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}\cancel{180} - 3 x + y & = & \cancel{180} \\ - 3 x + y & = & 0 \\ y & = & 3 x\end{aligned}$

$y=3x$ 
**Full method and all reasons clearly given**** [1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°. Form an equation in terms of *$x$* and *$y$*.*

> *Use the ratio  *$x:y=5:7$* to form a second equation in terms of *$x$* and *$y$*.*

$x:y\,5:7\,\,7x=5y$* *

> *Rearrange the second equation to find *$x$* in terms of *$y$*.*

$x=\frac{5y}{7}$*  *

> *Substitute  *$x=\frac{5y}{7}$* into the first equation.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{5 y}{7} + y & = & 180\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify and solve to find *$y$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{5 y}{7} + \frac{7 y}{7} & = & 180 \\ \frac{12 y}{7} & = & 180 \\ 12 y & = & 1260 \\ y & = & \frac{1260}{12} \\ y & = & 105 \circ \end{aligned}$*  *

> *Substitute  *$y=105$*  into the second equation.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{5 \left(105\right)}{7} = \frac{525}{7} = 75 \circ\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°. Form an equation in terms of *$x$* and *$w$*.*

$\left(x + 20\right) + w = 180 \circ$*   (Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral = 180°)*

> *Substitute  *$x=75^{\circ}$* into the this equation.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(75 + 20\right) + w & = & 180 \circ\end{aligned}$* *

> *Simplify and solve to find *$w$*.*

$\begin{aligned}95 + w & = & 180 \\ w & = & 180 - 95\end{aligned}$*  *

**[1]**

$w=85^{\circ}$** [1]**

![Circle with points T, P, Q on its edge. Line TR is tangent at T, RS is 3 cm, SQ is 5 cm, and TS is 8.5 cm. Diagram states not accurately drawn.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/circle-theorems/assets/002-circle-with-points-t-p-q-on-its-edge-line-tr-is-.png)

*P*, *Q*, *S* and *T* are points on a circle.
*TSR* and *PQR* are straight lines.

Work out the length of *PQ*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> This question is a classic use of the intersecting secants theorem. A secant is a line that intersects a circle at two points.
> 
> The theorem states:
> 
> $(\mathrm{external} \mathrm{segment} \mathrm{length} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{secant}A)\times(\mathrm{full} \mathrm{secant} \mathrm{length}A)\,=(\mathrm{external} \mathrm{segment} \mathrm{length} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{secant}B)\times(\mathrm{full} \mathrm{secant} \mathrm{length}B)$

> *Write out the intersecting secants theorem in the context of the question*

$RS\timesRT=QR\timesPR$

> *Substitute in the lengths of known line segments and simplify*

$\begin{aligned}3 \times \left(3 + 8 . 5\right) & = & 5 \times \left(5 + P Q\right) \\ 34 . 5 & = & 25 + 5 P Q\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Solve to calculate *$PQ$

$\begin{aligned}34 . 5 & = & 25 + 5 P Q \\ 34 . 5 - 25 & = & 5 P Q \\ 9 . 5 & = & 5 P Q \\ \frac{9 . 5}{5} & = & P Q\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

$PQ=1.9$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
![q3-veryhard-4-8-congurence-similarity-and-geometry-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/similarity-and-geometrical-proof/assets/001-q3-veryhard-4-8-congurence-similarity-and-geomet.png)

$PQRST$ is a regular pentagon. 
$R,U$ and $T$ are points on a circle, centre $O$. 
$QR$ and $PT$ are tangents to the circle. 
$RSU$ is a straight line.

Prove that $ST=UT$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To prove that **ST  **is equal to** UT ** you will need to **prove **that the triangle **STU **is **isosceles**. This can be done by finding the angles. *

> *PQRST **is a regular pentagon, so the angle **TSU** is the exterior angle of a regular pentagon. Exterior angles in any polygon add up to 360°. A regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles.*

> * *`T S with hat on top U space equals 360 over 5 equals space 72 degree`

**[1]**

> *To find the size of angle **SUT**, you will need to consider circle theorems.*

> *Begin by joining the point **O** to the points **T** and **R,** marking all the radiuses of the circle as equal lengths on the diagram.*

> *TP** and **TR **are also tangents to the circle, so by the circle theorem 'A tangent always meets a radius at 90°', angles **ORQ **and **OTP **are both 90°. *

`O R with hat on top Q space equals space O T with hat on top P space equals 90 degree`* **(angle between tangent and radius)*

**[1]**

> *Mark these onto the diagram.*

![QLY1pOQ2_4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/similarity-and-geometrical-proof/assets/002-qly1poq2-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2.png)

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2). A regular pentagon has 5 equal interior angles, therefore these can be found using the formula *$\frac{180 \left(5 - 2\right)}{5}$*.*

> * *$T \hat{P} Q = P \hat{Q} R = \frac{3 \left(180\right)}{5} = 108 \circ$

> *Add these angles to the diagram.*

![4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/similarity-and-geometrical-proof/assets/003-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3.png)

> *PQROT  **is a pentagon, so the angle **ROT**  can be found by subtracting the other four angles from the sun of the angles in a pentagon.*

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2).*

$R \hat{O} T + O \hat{T} P + T \hat{P} Q + P \hat{Q} R + Q \hat{R} O = 180 \left(5 - 2\right) \circ = 540 \circ$

> *Substitute in the angles you know to find angle **ROT**.*

$\begin{aligned}R \hat{O} T + 90 \circ + 90 \circ + 108 \circ + 108 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T + 396 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T & = & 144 \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *By the circle theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, angle **ROT **is twice angle **RUT.*

$R \hat{O} T = 2 \left(R \hat{U} T\right) = 2 \left(S \hat{U} T\right)$

$S \hat{U} T = \frac{R \hat{O} T}{2} = \frac{144}{2} = 72 \circ$

**[1]**

> *This proves that angle **TSU **is equal to angle **SUT **and so triangle **STU **is isosceles.*

**Therefore ****ST ****= ****UT **
**All reasons given clearly [1]**

$ABC$ and $AED$ are straight lines. 
$BE$ and $CD$ are parallel

. $BE=1.5\mathrm{cm}.\,CD=6\mathrm{cm}.\,AD=5\mathrm{cm}.$

Calculate the length of $ED$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The triangles are similar so there will exist a value of **k **such that  *$\begin{aligned}A D & = & k A E\end{aligned}$* and *$\begin{aligned}C D & = & k B E\end{aligned}$*. *
*k **is known as the scale factor.*

> *It may help to draw the two triangles out separately next to each other.*

![mz_sJ8_1_4-8-edexcel-gcse-eq5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/similarity-and-geometrical-proof/assets/041-mz-sj8-1-4-8-edexcel-gcse-eq5.png)

> *Form an equation using the two known sides of the triangle.*

$\begin{aligned}C D & = & k B E\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute the values of *$CD$* and *$BE$* into the equation and solve to find *$k$*.*

$\begin{aligned}6 & = & 1 . 5 k \\ k & = & \frac{6}{1 . 5} = 4\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute into *$\begin{aligned}A D & = & k A E\end{aligned}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A D & = & k A E \\ 5 & = & \left(4\right) A E\end{aligned}$

> *Solve to find *$AE$*.*

$\begin{aligned}5 & = & 4 A E \\ A E & = & \frac{5}{4} = 1 . 25\end{aligned}$

> $ED=AD-AE$*. Substitute the values of*$AD$* and*$AE$* in.*

$\begin{aligned}E D & = & A D - A E = 5 - 1 . 25 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$ED=3.75$** cm**** ****[1]**

The photo is 16 cm by 10 cm. 
The card is 30 cm by 15 cm.

Steve cuts the card along the dotted line shown in the diagram below.

![q3-2-hard-4-8-congurence-similarity-and-geometry-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/similarity-and-geometrical-proof/assets/026-q3-2-hard-4-8-congurence-similarity-and-geometry.png)

Steve throws away the piece of card that is 15 cm by $x$ cm. The piece of card he has left is mathematically similar to the photo.

Work out the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The piece of card is mathematically similar to the photo so there will exist a scale factor which can be used to find the length of one of the shapes, given the length of the other.*

> *Let the scale factor be **k**.*

> *Form an equation using the two known sides, these are the width of the photo and the width of the card.*

$\begin{aligned}W i d t h \left(c a r d\right) & = & k W i d t h \left(p h o t o\right) \\ 15 & = & 10 k\end{aligned}$

> *Solve to find *$k$*.*

$\begin{aligned}10 k & = & 15 \\ k & = & \frac{15}{10} = 1 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation for the length of the photo and the length of the card.*

$\begin{aligned}L e n g t h \left(c a r d\right) & = & k L e n g t h \left(p h o t o\right) \\ l & = & 16 k\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$k=1.5$* to find the length of the card.*

$\begin{aligned}l & = & 16 \left(1 . 5\right) \\ l & = & 24\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This is the length of the card after *$x$* cm has been cut from the original length of 30 cm.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 30 - l \\ x & = & 30 - 24\end{aligned}$

$x=6$** cm**** ****[1]**

The real height of tower $A$ is $187m$.

The height of tower $A$ on the scale model is $90\mathrm{cm}$.

Work out the height of tower $B$ on the scale model. 
Give your answer correct to the nearest centimetre.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The height of model **A** and the height of model **B** are corresponding lengths in similar shapes so find **k, **the scale factor, using**  *$\begin{aligned}k & = & \frac{second corresponding length}{first corresponding length}\end{aligned}$

> *Method 1*

> *The height of model **B** is smaller than the height of model **A**. **To go from the big shape to the small shape, put the small length on top in the fraction so that **k** will be smaller than 1*

$\begin{aligned}k & = & \frac{height \mathbf{B}}{height \mathbf{A}} = \frac{147}{187}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the height of model **B** by multiplying the height of model **A** by **k **(notice that **k** < 1 so multiplying by **k** will make the length smaller)*

$\begin{aligned}height \mathbf{B} & = & k \left[height \mathbf{A}\right] = \frac{147}{187} \times 90\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned} & = & 70 . 7486631 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *This answer is already in centimetres but give the final answer to the nearest centimetre as requested in the question*

**71 cm**** ****[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Finding **k **using**  *$\begin{aligned}k & = & \frac{second corresponding length}{first corresponding length}\end{aligned}$*, if you put the larger length on top of the fraction then;*

$\begin{aligned}k & = & \frac{height \mathbf{A}}{height \mathbf{B}} = \frac{187}{147} \end{aligned}$

> *Notice that **k** > 1 so multiplying by **k** will make the length bigger- but in going from the height of model **A** to the height of model of **B**, we want to go from a longer length to a smaller length. So divide by **k **instead*

$\begin{aligned}height \mathbf{B} & = & height \mathbf{A} \div k = 90 \div \frac{187}{147}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned} & = & 70 . 7486631 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *This answer is already in centimetres but give the final answer to the nearest centimetre as requested in the question*

**71 cm ****[1]**

**[1]**

> *Find radius of **B** by multiplying the radius of **A** by **k **(notice that **k** < 1 so multiplying by **k** will make the length smaller)*

$\begin{aligned}radius \mathbf{B} & = & k \left[radius \mathbf{A}\right] = \frac{3}{8} \times 0 . 56\end{aligned}$

**0.21 m**** ****[1]**

> *Finding **k **using**  *$\begin{aligned}k & = & \frac{second corresponding length}{first corresponding length}\end{aligned}$*, if you put the larger length on top of the fraction then;*

*Method 1* 
*The ratio of radii (lengths) is 1 : 2 so the ratio of volumes is 1*<sup>*3*</sup>* : 2*<sup>*3*</sup> *Split this volume up into the ratio 1 : 8 (by finding *$\frac{1}{9}$* of it and *$\frac{8}{9}$* of it*

$\begin{aligned}10^{2} & = & Q P^{2} + \left(4 \sqrt{5}\right)^{2} \\ 10^{2} - \left(4 \sqrt{5}\right)^{2} & = & Q P^{2} \\ \sqrt{10^{2} - \left(4 \sqrt{5}\right)^{2}} & = & Q P \\ \sqrt{100 - 80} & = & Q P \\ \sqrt{20} & = & Q P \\ 2 \sqrt{5} & = & Q P\end{aligned}$

**Triangles QRS and PQS are similar because they have three pairs of corresponding sides with the same ratio ****[1]**

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 6 \times 1 . 5 \\ & = & 9\end{aligned}$

**The third option is correct, 9 cm ****[1]**

> *The first option is greater than 6 but not in the correct scale factor because *$\frac{15}{10}\neq\frac{7.5}{6}$

> *The second option is greater than 6 but not in the correct scale factor because *$\frac{15}{10}\neq\frac{11}{6}$

The container is a cylinder on top of a cone.
The cylinder has a radius of 3 m and a height of $h$m.
The cone has a base radius of 3 m and a vertical height of 4 m.

The container is empty.
The container is then filled with grain at a constant rate.

After 5 hours the depth of the grain is 6 metres above the vertex of the cone.
After 9 hours the container is full of grain.

Work out the value of $h$.
Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the volume of grain that is poured into the container in the first 5 hours, by adding together the volume of the cone *$\left(V = \frac{1}{3} \pi r^{2} h\right)$* and the volume of a cylinder, *$\left(V = \pi r^{2} h\right)$*, of height 2m.*

![4-7-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/022-4-7-2.png)

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{1}{3} \pi \left(3\right)^{2} \left(4\right) + \pi \left(3\right)^{2} \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

**For correct substitution into the volume formula for either the cone or the cylinder ****[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{1}{3} \pi \times 36 + \pi \times 18 \\ & = & 12 \pi + 18 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 30 \pi m^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the rate of flow of the grain by dividing the volume of grain by the time taken to pour it.*

$\begin{aligned} & & \frac{30 \pi}{5} \\ & = & 6 \pi m^{3} h^{- 1}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the volume of grain that will be poured in 4 hours by multiplying the rate of flow of the grain by 4.*

$\begin{aligned} & & 6 \pi \times 4 \\ & = & 24 \pi m^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The grain poured in the last 4 hours will just fill the remainder of the cylinder, so calculate the height of the remainder of the cylinder that is filled by substituting the volume into the formula for the volume of a cylinder.*

$\begin{aligned}24 \pi & = & \pi \left(3\right)^{2} h\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}24 \pi & = & 9 \pi h \\ \frac{24}{9} & = & h \\ h & = & \frac{8}{3} m\end{aligned}$

> *Work out the value of *$h$* by adding together the height of the cylindrical parts from the two volumes.*

$\begin{aligned}h & = & 2 + \frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}$

$\frac{14}{3}m$* ***[1]**

**Leave your working in terms of **$π$** throughout, in a non-calculator paper question it will frequently cancel out.**

parts.problemMd:

![q1-4-7-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/047-q1-4-7-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The cylinder has base radius $2x$ and height $9x$.

The cylinder is melted down and made into a sphere of radius $r$.

Find an expression for $r$ in terms of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *If the cylinder is melted down and reformed into a sphere, then the cylinder and sphere will have the same volume.*

> *Calculate the volume of the cylinder, using the formula: *$V=πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the cylinder and *$h$*is its height.  *

> *Leave your answer in terms of *$π$*.*

$V = \pi \times \left(2 x\right)^{2} \times 9 x$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \pi \times 4 x^{2} \times 9 x \\ & = & 36 \pi x^{3} cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Using the formula for the volume of a sphere: *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the sphere, substitute the calculated value for the volume and rearrange to find an expression for the radius of the sphere.*

$36πx^{3}=\frac{4}{3}π\timesr^{3}\,$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by *$π$*.*

$36x^{3}=\frac{4}{3}r^{3}$

> *Divide both sides by 4.*

$9x^{3}=\frac{1}{3}r^{3}$

> *Multiply both sides by 3.*

$27x^{3}=r^{3}$

> *Take the cube root of both sides.*

$3x=r$

$3x$* ***[1]**

**Final answer:** **Any algebraic expression equivalent to **$3x$** will be accepted**

> *The large and small cones are similar objects.*

$\mathrm{LSF}=\frac{40}{20}=2$

> *Divide the radius of the large cone by the LSF to work out the radius of the small cone.*

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 2625 \pi \\ & = & 8246 . 68071 . . . cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}A_{t o t a l} & = & 288 \pi \\ & = & 904 . 778684 . . . cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

![q6-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/068-q6-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The radius of the hemisphere is 4 cm.
The radius of the base of the cone is 4 cm.

Calculate the volume of the solid.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Work out the perpendicular height of the cone by subtracting the radius of the hemisphere from the total height of the object.*

$\begin{aligned}h & = & 14 - 4 \\ & = & 10 cm\end{aligned}$

![4-7-8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/069-4-7-8.png)

> *Calculate the volume of the sphere, using the formula: *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*, where *$r$* is the radius, and divide the result by 2 to calculate the volume of the hemisphere.*

> *It is a good idea to keep your answer in terms of *$π$* to avoid rounding errors.*

$V_{Hemisphere}=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{4}{3}π\times4^{3}$

**[1]**

$V_{Hemisphere}=\frac{128}{3}π$

> *Calculate the volume of the cone, using the formula: *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$V_{Cone}=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\times4^{2}\times10$

**[1]**

$V_{Cone}=\frac{160}{3}π$

> *Find the total volume of the solid by adding together the volume of the hemisphere and the volume of the cone.*

$V_{Solid}=\frac{128}{3}π+\frac{160}{3}π$

$\begin{aligned}V_{S o l i d} & = & 96 \pi \\ & = & 301 . 59289 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

$302\mathrm{cm}^{3}$* ***[1]**

**Answers between the values of 301 to 302 will be accepted. Answer of **$96π$** and **$\frac{288}{3}π$** will also be accepted.**

parts.problemMd:

Work out the volume of the cylinder.

parts.solutionMd:
*The formula for the the volume of a cylinder is *$V=πr^{2}h$* where **r** is the length of the radius and **h** is the height. The radius is half of the diameter.*

> *Substitute **r** = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 and **h** = 20 into the formula.*

> $\begin{aligned}V & = & \pi \times 7^{2} \times 20 \\ & = & 980 \pi \\ & = & 3078 . 76080 . . .\end{aligned}$*  *

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**Volume is 3080 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** (3sf)**** ****[1] **

parts.problemMd:
A frustum is made by removing a small cone from a large cone. The cones are mathematically similar.

![q16-paper1h-june2018-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/019-q16-paper1h-june2018-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

The large cone has base radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm. Given that

$\frac{\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{frustum}}{\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{large} \mathrm{cone}}=\frac{98}{125}$

find an expression, in terms of $h$, for the height of the frustum.

....................................................... cm
parts.solutionMd:
> *First sketch a diagram of a side view of the cones and frustum. We will let the height of the frustum be *$f$*, the height of the small cone be *$H$* and the radius of the small cone be *$R$

![edexcel-tq-mis-area-and-volume-similar-shapes-vh-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/020-edexcel-tq-mis-area-and-volume-similar-shapes-vh.png)

> *We need *$f$* and we can see that *$f=h-H$*. So we need *$H$* in terms of *$h$

> *If *$\frac{98}{125}$* represents the fraction of the large cone that the frustum occupies, then the fraction of the large cone that the small cone occupies is *

$1-\frac{98}{125}=\frac{27}{125}$

**[1]**

> *This *$\frac{27}{125}$* is effectively the scale factor of the small cone to the large cone*

> *Therefore if we cube root *$\frac{27}{125}$*, we have the length scale factor of the small cone to the large cone*

$\sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{125}} = \frac{3}{5}$

**[1]**

> *Therefore *

$H=\frac{3}{5}h$

> *And*

$\begin{aligned}f & = & h - H \\ & = & h - \frac{3}{5} h\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

**The height of the frustum is **$\begin{aligned} & & \frac{2}{5} \mathbf{\mathit{h}}\end{aligned}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Jane makes cheese. The cheese is in the shape of a cuboid.

![q7-1-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/070-q7-1-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

Jane is going to make a new cheese.

The new cheese will also be in the shape of a cuboid. 
The cross section of the cuboid will be a 5 cm by 5 cm square.

![q7-2-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/071-q7-2-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

Jane wants the new cuboid to have the same volume as the 2 cm by 10 cm by 15 cm cuboid.

Work out the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the volume of the cheese, using the formula: *$V=l\timesw\timesh$*, where *$l$* is the length of the cuboid, *$w$*is the width and *$h$* is the height.*

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 15 \times 10 \times 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 300 cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute the resultant volume and the known dimensions of the new cheese into the formula for the volume of a cuboid and solve to find the length of the new cheese.*

$300=x\times5\times5$

> *Simplify.*

$300=25x$

$12\mathrm{cm}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A cylinder has height 1.6 m and radius 0.56 m.  
Work out the curved surface area of the cylinder.

parts.solutionMd:
> *The the curved surface area of a cylinder is the part of the cylinder that when unrolled would be a rectangle, with the width equal to the height of the cylinder and the length equal to the circumference of the base circle of the cylinder.*

> *Find the circumference of the base of the cylinder using the formula *$C=2πr$* where **r** is the radius.*

> $\begin{aligned}circumference & = & 2 \pi \times 0 . 56\end{aligned}$*  *

> *Find the curved surface area of the cylinder by multiplying the circumference with the height.*

> $\begin{aligned}C S A & = & 2 \pi \times 0 . 56 \times 1 . 6\end{aligned}$*  *

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**CSA is 5.63 m**<sup>**2**</sup>** (3sf)*** ***[1] **

parts.problemMd:
Here is a sector, $AOB$ , of a circle with centre $O$and angle $AOB$= $x^{\circ}$

![q26-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/033-q26-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The sector can form the curved surface of a cone by joining $OA$to $OB$ .

![q26-14ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/034-q26-14ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The height of the cone is $25\mathrm{cm}$.
The volume of the cone is $1600\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

Work out the value of $x.$ 
Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

$x=$.......................
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the volume of a cone, *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*, is given at the beginning of the paper. Use the formula with the given volume of the cone to find the value of the radius of the base circle. *

> *Using the known volume of 1600 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* we can write the following equation.*

$\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\timesr^{2}\times25=1600$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 25 and *$\frac{1}{3}π$*.*

$\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}=\frac{1600}{25}=64$

$r^{2}=\frac{64}{\frac{π}{3}}=\frac{192}{π}=61.11549...$

> *Square root both sides.*

$r=\sqrt{61.11549...}=7.817640...$

**[1]**

> *The formula for the curved surface area of a cone, *$πrl$* , is given at the beginning of the paper.*

> *Use Pythagoras' Theorem to find the value of *$l$*, the slant height of the cone. *

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q6-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/035-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q6-diagram-1.png)

> *It is a right angled triangle so you can use Pythagoras' Theorem: *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*, where **c** is the length of the hypotenuse (the slant height) and **a** and **b **are the height and the radius. *

$\begin{aligned}l^{2} & = & 7 . 81764 . . .^{2} + 25^{2} \\ l & = & \sqrt{7 . 81764 . . .^{2} + 25^{2}} \\ & = & 26 . 193806 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the values of *$l$* and *$r$* into the formula for the curved surface area of a cone.*

$\begin{aligned}C S A & = & \pi r l = \pi \left(7 . 817640 . . .\right) \left(26 . 193806 . . .\right) = 643 . 313706 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The area of the sector is equal to the curved surface area of the cone. Use the formula for area of a sector *$\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*, where the radius of the sector is equal to the slant height of the cone, to find the value of the angle, *$x$*.*

$\frac{x}{360} \times \pi \times \begin{aligned} & & 26\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 193806\end{aligned} . . .^{2} = \begin{aligned} & & 643\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 313706\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{360} & = & \frac{643 . 313706 . . .}{ 26 . 193806 . . .^{2} \times \pi } \\ \frac{x}{360} & = & 0 . 298452 . . . \\ x & = & 0 . 298452 . . . \times 360 = 107 . 4430 . . .\end{aligned}$

$x=107^{\circ}$ **[1]**

**Rounded to 3 significant figures 107 - 108 allowed**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a solid shape.

![q9-4-7-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/040-q9-4-7-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The solid shape is made from a hemisphere and a cone.
The radius of the hemisphere is equal to the radius of the base of the cone.

The cone has a height of 10 cm.
The volume of the cone is 270$π$ cm<sup>3</sup>.

Work out the total volume of the solid shape.
Give your answer in terms of $π$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute the value given for the volume of the cone into the formula for the volume of a cone: *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the cone and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$270π=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\timesr^{2}\times10$

**[1]**

> *Solve to find the radius.*

$\begin{aligned}270 \pi & = & \frac{10}{3} \pi r^{2} \\ 270 & = & \frac{10}{3} r^{2} \\ 27 & = & \frac{1}{3} r^{2} \\ 81 & = & r^{2} \\ r & = & 9 cm\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the volume of the volume of the hemisphere by substituting the value for the radius into the formula for the volume of a sphere and multiplying the result by *$\frac{1}{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 9^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{2}{3} \times \pi \times 729 \\ & = & 2 \times \pi \times 243 \\ & = & 486 \pi cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Add the volume of the hemisphere to the volume of the cone to find the total volume of the shape.*

$V_{total}=270π+486π$

**[1]**

$756π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Anne wants to fill 12 hanging baskets with compost.

Each hanging basket is a hemisphere of diameter 40 cm.

Anne has 4 bags of compost. 
There are 50 litres of compost in each bag.

Has Anne got enough compost to fill the 12 hanging baskets?

![q8-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/066-q8-4-7-medium-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the radius, *$r$*, of the sphere by halving the diameter.*

$r=\frac{40}{2}=20\mathrm{cm}$

> *If there are twelve hemispherical hanging baskets, the volume of these would be equivalent to six spheres of the same radius. Calculate the volume of six spheres of radius 20 cm, using the formula: *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 6 \times \frac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 20^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 64 000 \pi \\ & = & 201061 . 929 . . . cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Convert the amount of compost in one bag from litres to cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*.*

*1 litre = 1 000 cm**<sup>3</sup>*

*50 litres = 50 000 cm**<sup>3</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Work out the total amount of compost that Anne has in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*.*

$4\times50000=200000\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

**[1]**

**No, Anne does not have enough compost as she needs 201 062 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** but only has 200 000 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A solid, $S$, is made from a hemisphere and a cylinder.

The centre of the circular face of the hemisphere and the centre of the top face of the cylinder are at the same point.

![q17-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/016-q17-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

The radius of the cylinder and the radius of the hemisphere are both $x$ cm.

The height of the cylinder is $(20--4x)\mathrm{cm}.$

The volume of $S$ is $V$cm<sup>3</sup> where $V=\frac{1}{3}πy$

Find the maximum value of $y$. 
Show clear algebraic working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the volume of S by adding together the volume of a cylinder ("*$V=πr^{2}h$*") and the volume of the hemisphere (half the volume of a sphere so "*$V=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*").*

$V = \pi \left(x\right)^{2} \left(20 - 4 x\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \left(x\right)^{3}\right)$

**[1]**

> *Equate this to the given expression for the volume of S, and simplify to make things easier.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \pi y & = & \pi \left(x\right)^{2} \left(20 - 4 x\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \left(x\right)^{3}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \pi y & = & 20 \pi x^{2} - 4 \pi x^{3} + \frac{2}{3} \pi x^{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \pi y & = & 20 \pi x^{2} - \frac{10}{3} \pi x^{3} \\ \pi y & = & 60 \pi x^{2} - 10 \pi x^{3} \\ \cancel{\pi} y & = & 10 \cancel{\pi} x^{2} \left(6 - x\right) \\ y & = & 10 x^{2} \left(6 - x\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *To find the maximum value of y we need to use differentiation.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 60 x^{2} - 10 x^{3} \\ \frac{d y}{d x} & = & 120 x - 30 x^{2} \\ \frac{d y}{d x} & = & 30 x \left(4 - x\right)\end{aligned}$

> *At a maximum value, *$\frac{dy}{dx}=0$*.*

$30x\left(4 - x\right)= 0$
$\cancel{x = 0} , x = 4$

**[1]**

> *Reject *$x=0$* as a solution since the radius of the hemisphere and cylinder cannot be zero! *

> *So *$x=4$* (we can assume) is the **x** value at the maximum for **y**. Substitute this into our equation for **y** in terms of **x**.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 10 \times 4^{2} \times \left(6 - 4\right) \\ y & = & 10 \times 16 \times 2 \\ y & = & 320\end{aligned}$

**Therefore the maximum value of ****y**** is 320*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows an oil tan in the shape of a prism. 
The cross section of the prism is a trapezium.

![screenshot-2023-05-26-at-2-22-08-pm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/055-screenshot-2023-05-26-at-2-22-08-pm.png)

The tank is empty.

Oil flows into the tank. 
After one minute there are 300 litres of oil in the tank.

Assume that oil continues to flow into the tank at this rate.

Work out how many **more** minutes it takes for the tank to be 85% full of oil. (1m<sup>3 </sup>= 1000 litres)
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the cross-section of the tank, using the formula for the area of a trapezium: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel sides and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \left(3 + 1 . 4\right) \times 2 . 4\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 5 . 28 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the volume of the tank by multiplying the cross-sectional area by the length of the tank.*

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 5 . 28 \times 2 . 5 \\ & = & 13 . 2 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide the given percentage by 100 and multiply it by the volume to calculate the volume of oil required to fill the tank up to 85% capacity.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{85 \%} & = & \frac{85}{100} \times 13 . 2 \\ & = & 11 . 22 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Convert the volume of oil required in m*<sup>*3*</sup>* to litres by multiplying the volume in m*<sup>*3*</sup>* by 1000.*

*1000 litres = 1 m**<sup>3</sup>*

$\begin{aligned}V_{85 \%} & = & 11 . 22 \times 1000 \\ & = & 11220 litres\end{aligned}$

The trapezium $ABCD$, in which $AD$ is parallel to $BC$, is a cross section of the prism.

The base $ADEH$ of the prism is a horizontal plane.
$ADEH$ and $BCFG$ are rectangles.
The midpoint of $BC$ is vertically above the midpoint of $AD$ so that $BA=CD$.

$AD=37\mathrm{cm}$   $GF=28\mathrm{cm}$    $DE=24\mathrm{cm}$

The perpendicular distance between edges $AD$ and $BC$ is 20 $\mathrm{cm}$.

Work out the total surface area of the prism.
parts.solutionMd:
*To find the total surface area we need to find the area of the individual 2D shapes that make up the prism.* 
*There are two congruent (identical) trapeziums.*
*Two congruent rectangles making up the 'sloping' sides (left and right as we look at the diagram).*
*A rectangle for the 'top' and a different rectangle for the base.*

*It may help to draw a net of the prism.  It does not need to be accurate.* 
*We do not know the length of the sloping side so we shall call that **x** for now.*

![C6XhjQIv_edx-igcse-pptq-vol-surf-area-vh-q10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/027-c6xhjqiv-edx-igcse-pptq-vol-surf-area-vh-q10.png)

> *So using the standard formulae for the area of trapeziums and rectangles we can write down a formula for the total surface area, **S** say, of the prism.*

$\begin{aligned}S & = & 2 \times \left(\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times \left(37 + 28\right)\right) + 2 \times \left(24 \times x\right) + \left(24 \times 28\right) + \left(24 \times 37\right) \\ S & = & 1300 + 48 x + 672 + 888 \\ S & = & 2860 + 48 x\end{aligned}$

**Method for area of a trapezium ****[1]** 
**Method for total surface area ****[1]**

*To find the value of **x** we can use Pythagoras' theorem ("*$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}$*") on the 'triangular' part of the prism **ABCD**.*

> *We also need the base of this triangle - as the trapezium is isosceles this is found by*

$\frac{37-28}{2}=4.5$

> *Sketching a diagram can help.*

![4dyd4fS-_edx-igcse-pptq-vol-surf-area-vh-q10-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/028-4dyd4fs-edx-igcse-pptq-vol-surf-area-vh-q10-2.png)

$\begin{aligned}\therefore x^{2} & = & 20^{2} + 4 . 5^{2} \\ x^{2} & = & 420 . 25 \\ x & = & 20 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we can complete our calculation to find the total surface area of the prism.*

$\begin{aligned}S & = & 2860 + 48 x \\ S & = & 2860 + 48 \times 20 . 5 \\ S & = & 3844\end{aligned}$

**The total surface area of the prism is 3844 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1]**

*ABC** is a right-angled triangle, where **AB **= 5 cm, **BC** = 12 cm.*

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem with triangle**ABC **to find the length of **AC**.*

*  *$AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}\,AC^{2}=5^{2}+12^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Solve**.*

$\begin{aligned}A C^{} & = & \sqrt{5^{2} + 12^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{169} \\ & = & 13\end{aligned}$

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem with triangle**ACM **to find the length of **CM**.*

**  **$\begin{aligned}A M^{ 2 } & = & A C^{ 2 } + C M^{ 2} \\ 16^{ 2 } & = & 13^{2} + C M^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find **CM.*

$\begin{aligned}C \left(M^{2}\right)^{} & = & 16^{2} - 13^{2} \\ C M & = & \sqrt{16^{2} - 13^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{87}\end{aligned}$

**  **$\begin{aligned}C F & = & 2 C M = 2 \sqrt{87}\end{aligned}$

> *Find the volume of the prism by multiplying the area of the cross-section (triangle **ABC**) by the length of the prism (**CF**). The area of a right-angled triangle can be found multiplying the base by the height and dividing by 2. *

$\begin{aligned}Volume^{} & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(5\right) \left(12\right) \times 2 \sqrt{87} = 559 . 6427 . . . cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *The total surface area of the solid shape is made up of the two curved surface areas of each cone added together.  Substitute the radius and slant height for each into the given formula for the curved surface area, *$πrl$*.*

$\begin{aligned}CSA_{smaller cone} & = & \pi \times r \times 2 r = 2 r^{2} \pi\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}CSA_{bigger cone} & = & \pi \times r \times 3 r = 3 r^{2} \pi\end{aligned}$

**Either expression correct ****[1]**

> *Add the two curved surface areas together to form an expression for the total surface area of the shape.*

$\begin{aligned}2 \pi r^{2} + 3 \pi r^{2} & = & 5 \pi r^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Form an equation by setting this expression equal to the value given for the total surface area of the shape.*

$5πr^{2}=57.8π$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}5 r^{2} & = & 57 . 8\end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by 5.*

> *Square root both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}r & = & \sqrt{11 . 56} = 3 . 4\end{aligned}$

$r=3.4\mathrm{cm}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A cone has a volume of $562.5π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$.

The radius of the base of the cone is equal to twice the height of the cone.

parts.solutionMd:
> *Using the variable, **h**, for height allows the radius to be expressed as 2**h** as shown below:*

![Illustration of a right circular cone with height labelled "h," diameter "2h," and a right angle at the base centre.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/001-illustration-of-a-right-circular-cone-with-heigh.png)

> *Substitute the known values and variables  into the formula for the volume of a cone, *$\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$* to form an equation*

$\frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times \left(2 h\right)^{2} \times h = 562 . 5 \pi$

**[M1]**

> *Simplify terms on the left side of the equation*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 4 h^{2} \times h & = & 562 . 5 \pi \\ \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 4 h^{3} & = & 562 . 5 \pi \\ \frac{4}{3} \pi h^{3} & = & 562 . 5 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Divide through by *$π$

$\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} h^{3} & = & 562 . 5\end{aligned}$

> *Continue to solve the equation for *$h$

$\begin{aligned}4 h^{3} & = & 3 \times 562 . 5 \\ h^{3} & = & \frac{1687 . 5}{4} \\ h & = & \sqrt[3]{421 . 875} \\ h & = & 7 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Since *$h=7.5$* then *$2h=15$* which is the length of the radius of the cone*

> *Substitute these values into Pythagoras' theorem (*$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*) to calculate the length of the sloping edge of the cone, *$l$

![Diagram of a right circular cone with a height of 7.5 units and a base radius of 15 units, showing a perpendicular from the vertex to the base.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-modular-24-higher-unit-2/geometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/002-diagram-of-a-right-circular-cone-with-a-height-o.png)

$\begin{aligned}7 . 5^{2} + 15^{2} & = & l^{2} \\ 56 . 25 + 225 & = & l^{2} \\ 281 . 25 & = & l^{2} \\ \sqrt{281 . 25} & = & l \\ l & = & 16 . 770 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Substitute values into the formula for the curved surface area of a cone, *$πrl$

$π\times15\times\sqrt{281.25}=790.291...$

> *Round to 3 significant figures as stated in the question*

**Final answer:** **790**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The final mark is awarded for answers in the range 786.5 to 791.7

[3]

> *Substitute the values into the formula for compound interest.*

*Formula for compound interest *$A = P \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^{n}$*A** = final amount = 206.46* 
*P  =** initial amount = 200* 
*r**  =  interest rate = **r* 
*n** = number of years = 2.*
*Substitute the values into the formula to form an equation.   *

$200 \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^{2} = 206 . 46$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 200.  *

$( 1 + \frac{r}{100} ) ^{2} = \frac{206.46}{200}$
$( 1 + \frac{r}{100} ) ^{2} = 1.0323$

> * Expand the brackets by multiplying every term in the first bracket by every term in the second bracket.   *

$\begin{aligned}\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right) \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right) & = & 1 . 0323 \\ 1 \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right) + \frac{r}{100} \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right) & = & 1 . 0323 \\ 1 + \frac{r}{100} + \frac{r}{100} + \left(\frac{r}{100}\right)^{2} & = & 1 . 0323 \\ 1 + \frac{2 r}{100} + \left(\frac{r}{100}\right)^{2} & = & 1 . 0323\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Set equal to zero and rearrange. *

> *      *$\begin{aligned}1 + \frac{2 r}{100} + \left(\frac{r}{100}\right)^{2} - 1 . 0323 & = & 0 \\ \left(\frac{r}{100}\right)^{2} + \frac{2 r}{100} - 0 . 0323 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

> *    Remove the fractions by multiplying every term by 100*<sup>*2*</sup>* .  *

$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{r}{100}\right)^{2} \left(100\right)^{2} + \frac{2 r}{100} \left(100\right)^{2} - 0 . 0323 \left(100\right)^{2} & = & 0 \\ \frac{10000 r^{2}}{10000} + \frac{200000 r}{100} - 323 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

$r^{2}+200r-323=0$ **[1]***   *

parts.problemMd:
The table shows a set of values for $x$ and $y$.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | $9$ | $2\frac{1}{4}$ | $1$ | $\frac{9}{16}$ |

$y$ is inversely proportional to the square of $x$.

Find an equation for $y$ in terms of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the inverse proportion relationship  *$y=\frac{k}{x^{2}}$*,  and substitute in **any one** pair of corresponding **x** and **y** values from the table.  (Pick the pair that will make your calculations the easiest!) Then solve the equation to find the value of **k**.*

$\begin{aligned}9 & = & \frac{k}{1^{2}} \\ 9 \times 1^{2} & = & k \\ 9 \times 1 & = & k \\ 9 & = & k\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now give the equation for **y** with that value of **k** inserted**.*

$y=\frac{9}{x^{2}}$**  [1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the positive value of $x$ when $y=16$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute **y **= 16 into the equation from part (a). Then rearrange and solve to find the corresponding value of **x**.*

$\begin{aligned}16 & = & \frac{9}{x^{2}} \\ 16 \times x^{2} & = & 9 \\ x^{2} & = & 9 \div 16 \\ x^{2} & = & \frac{9}{16} \\ x & = & \sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} \\ x & = & \pm \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$x=\frac{3}{4}$**  [1]**

**Be sure to give the ****positive**** value of ****x****, as asked for in the question.**

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Yesterday it took $5$ cleaners $4\frac{1}{2}$  hours to clean all the rooms in a hotel.

There are only $3$ cleaners to clean all the rooms in the hotel today.

Each cleaner is paid £$8.20$ for each hour or part of an hour they work.

How much will each cleaner be paid today?
parts.solutionMd:
> *It may not be obvious at first, but this is an inverse proportion question.  *
*The number of hours spent by each cleaner is inversely proportional to the number of cleaners.*
*Use the inverse proportion relationship  *$y=\frac{k}{x}$*,  with **y** as the number of hours per cleaner and **x**as the number of cleaners Then use the numbers in the question to find the value of**k**.*

$\begin{aligned}4 . 5 & = & \frac{k}{5} \\ 4 . 5 \times 5 & = & k \\ 22 . 5 & = & k\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now use the value of **k** to find the number of hours spent by each cleaner when the number of cleaners is 3.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & \frac{22 . 5}{3} \\ y & = & 7 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Be careful now!  The cleaners are paid £8.20 for each hour **or part of an hour** that they work.  *
*So you need to multiply £8.20 by **8** to find the amount each cleaner will be paid. *
*Remember to give your final answer to 2 decimal places, as we are talking about money.*

$\begin{aligned}8 . 20 \times 8 & = & 65 . 6\end{aligned}$

**£65.60****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
$y$ is directly proportional to $\sqrt[3]{x}$

$y=1\frac{1}{6}$ when  $x=8$

Find the value of $y$ when $x=64$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the direct proportion relationship  *$y = k \sqrt[3]{x}$*,  and substitute in the known values of **x** and **y**.*

$\begin{aligned}1 \frac{1}{6} & = & k \times \sqrt[3]{8}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now solve that equation to find the value of **k**.  Note that  *$2^{3}=8$*,  therefore  *$\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{6} & = & k \times 2 \\ \frac{7}{6} \div 2 & = & k \\ \frac{7}{12} & = & k\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now use the equation with that value of **k** and the new value of **x** to find the corresponding value of **y.**  Note that  *$4^{3}=64$*,  therefore  *$\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$*.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & \frac{7}{12} \times \sqrt[3]{64}\end{aligned}$

$y=\frac{7}{3}$**  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
$y$ is inversely proportional to $d^{2}$ 
When $d=10,y=4$

$d$ is directly proportional to $x^{2}$ 
When $x=2,d=24$

Find a formula for $y$ in terms of $x$. 
Give your answer in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the inverse proportion relationship  *$y=\frac{k_{1}}{d^{2}}$*,  and substitute in the known corresponding values of **y** and **d**. *
*Be careful!  There are two different constants of proportionality in this question. *
*We'll call the one connecting **y** and **d **in this part *$k_{1}$*, to distinguish it from the constant that connects **x** and **d**.*

$\begin{aligned}4 & = & \frac{k_{1}}{10^{2}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now solve that equation to find the value of *$k_{1}$* and use that value to write an equation for **y** in terms of **d**.*

$\begin{aligned}4 \times 10^{2} & = & k_{1} \\ 4 \times 100 & = & k_{1} \\ 400 & = & k_{1} \\ & & \\ y & = & \frac{400}{d^{2}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Next use the direct proportion relationship  *$d=k_{2}x^{2}$*,  and substitute in the known corresponding values of **x** and **d**.  (We use *$k_{2}$* here to represent the constant of proportionality connecting **x** and **d**.) *
*Solve that equation to find the value of *$k_{2}$*, and use that value to write an equation for **d** in terms of **x**.*

$\begin{aligned}24 & = & k_{2} \times 2^{2} \\ 24 & = & 4 k_{2} \\ \frac{24}{4} & = & k_{2} \\ 6 & = & k_{2} \\ & & \\ d & = & 6 x^{2 }\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now substitute that expression for **d** into the equation  *$\begin{aligned}y & = & \frac{400}{d^{2}}\end{aligned}$*  from above.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & \frac{400}{\left(6 x^{2}\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Finally, expand the brackets and simplify to get the final answer. Note that  *$\left(6 x^{2}\right)^{2} = 6^{2} \times \left(x^{2}\right)^{2} = 36 x^{4}$*.*

$y=\frac{400}{36x^{4}}\,\,y=\frac{4\times100}{4\times9x^{4}}$

$y=\frac{100}{9x^{4}}$**  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
A pendulum of length $L$ cm has time period $T$ seconds. 
$T$ is directly proportional to the square root of $L$.

The length of the pendulum is increased by 40%.

Work out the percentage increase in the time period.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First of all, note that we are not given any corresponding pairs of values for **T** and **L**.  Therefore we'll need to answer this question without finding the value of the constant of proportionality **k. **Start by writing down the direct proportion relationship  *$T=k\times\sqrt{L}$*,  using *$T_{1}$* to represent the initial period and *$L_{1}$* to represent the original length.*

$\begin{aligned}T_{1} & = & k \times \sqrt{L_{1}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now write down the equation for the situation after the length is increased. *
*Call the new period *$T_{2}$*. *
*Increasing a quantity by 40% is the same as multiplying it by 1.4, so the new length will be  *$1.4L_{1}$*. *
*Remember that  *$T_{1}=k\times\sqrt{L_{1}}$*  (from above), and also that by the laws of surds  *$\sqrt{1.4L_{1}}=\sqrt{1.4}\times\sqrt{L_{1}}$* .*

$\begin{aligned}T_{2} & = & k \times \sqrt{1 . 4 L_{1}} \\ T_{2} & = & k \times \sqrt{1 . 4} \times \sqrt{L_{1}} \\ T_{2} & = & \sqrt{1 . 4} \times \left(k \times \sqrt{L_{1}}\right) \\ T_{2} & = & \sqrt{1 . 4} \times T_{1}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Finally, use your calculator to find the value of *$\sqrt{1.4}$* and interpret that multiplier as a percentage increase.*

$\begin{aligned}T_{2} & = & 1 . 183215 . . . \times T_{1}\end{aligned}$

**18.3% increase (3 s.f.)****  [1]**

**Answers from 18.3 to 18.4 would get you the mark here.**

Assuming  *$k>0$*,  **y** is going to be positive when **x** is positive, and negative when **x** is negative.  So that has to be graph A.*
